blocks.html:
EXPOSÉ XXI
ROOT DATAby M. Demazure
In the absence of a suitable reference, this exposé collects together known results on root data (= "abstract" root systems), most of which will be used in what follows.

Notations. — We denote by \(\mathbb{Q}_+\) the set of positive (or zero) rational numbers; we have \(\mathbb{Z} \cap \mathbb{Q}_+ = \mathbb{N}\). Let \(V\) be a \(\mathbb{Q}\)-vector space; if \(A\) (resp. \(B\)) is a subset of \(\mathbb{Q}\) (resp. \(V\)), we denote by \(A \cdot B\) the image of \(A \otimes B\) under the morphism \(\mathbb{Q} \otimes V \to V\), in other words the set of linear combinations of elements of \(B\) with coefficients in \(A\). We write \(-B = \{-1\}B\). We denote by \(E - F\) the set \(\complement_{E}^{F}\).
1. Generalities
1.1. Definitions, first properties

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.1.1

Let \(M\) and \(M^*\) be two free \(\mathbb{Z}\)-modules of finite type in duality. We write \(V = M \otimes \mathbb{Q}\), \(V^* = M^* \otimes \mathbb{Q}\); these are two \(\mathbb{Q}\)-vector spaces in duality. We identify \(M\) (resp. \(M^*\)) with a subset of \(V\) (resp. \(V^*\)). The canonical bilinear form on \(M^* \times M\) (resp. \(V^* \times V\)) is denoted \((\ ,\ )\).

Let \(R\) be a finite subset of \(M\). Let us give ourselves a map \(\alpha \mapsto \alpha^*\) from \(R\) into \(M^*\); the set of the \(\alpha^*\), \(\alpha \in R\), is denoted \(R^*\). To each \(\alpha \in R\) we associate the endomorphism \(s_\alpha\) (resp. \(s^*_\alpha\)) of \(M\) and \(V\) (resp. \(M^*\) and \(V^*\)) given by the formulas: \[ (1)\qquad s_\alpha(x) = x - (\alpha^*, x)\alpha, \qquad \text{i.e.}\quad s_\alpha = \mathrm{id} - \alpha^* \otimes \alpha\,; \] \[ (1^*)\qquad s^*_\alpha(u) = u - (u, \alpha)\alpha^*, \qquad \text{i.e.}\quad s^*_\alpha = \mathrm{id} - \alpha \otimes \alpha^*. \] We say that the pair \((R, R^*)\) (more precisely the pair \((R, R \to M^*)\)) is a root datum in \((M, M^*)\), or that \((M, M^*, R, R^*)\) is a root datum, if the following axioms are satisfied:

(DR I) For each \(\alpha \in R\), we have \((\alpha^*, \alpha) = 2\).

(DR II) For each \(\alpha \in R\), we have \(s_\alpha(R) \subset R\), \(s^*_\alpha(R^*) \subset R^*\).
We say that \(R\) is the root system of the root datum \(\mathscr{R} = (M, M^*, R, R^*)\). The elements of \(R\) (resp. \(R^*\)) are called the roots (resp. coroots) of the root datum.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 1.1.2

Axiom (DR I) is equivalent to any one of the following properties: \[ (2)\quad s_\alpha s_\alpha = \mathrm{id}\ , \qquad (2^*)\quad s^*_\alpha s^*_\alpha = \mathrm{id}, \] \[ (3)\quad s_\alpha(\alpha) = -\alpha\ , \qquad (3^*)\quad s^*_\alpha(\alpha^*) = -\alpha^*. \]

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 1.1.3

Axioms (DR I) and (DR II) imply \[ R = -R, \qquad R^* = -R^*, \qquad 0 \notin R, \qquad 0 \notin R^*. \]

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.1.4

The map \(R \to R^*\) is a bijection. More generally, if \((\alpha^*, x) = (\beta^*, x)\) for all \(x \in R\), then \(\alpha = \beta\).

We then have \(s_\beta(\alpha) = \alpha - 2\beta\), \(s_\alpha(\beta) = \beta - 2\alpha\). One deduces at once \(s_\beta s_\alpha(\alpha) = \alpha + 2(\beta - \alpha)\), \(s_\beta s_\alpha(\beta - \alpha) = \beta - \alpha\), whence \((s_\beta s_\alpha)^n \alpha = \alpha + 2n(\beta - \alpha) \in R\) by (DR II). Since \(R\) is finite, we have \(\beta - \alpha = 0\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.1.5

The inverse map \(R^* \to R\) defines a root datum \[ \mathscr{R}^* = (M^*, M, R^*, R) \] called the dual of \(\mathscr{R}\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.1.6

We denote by \(\Gamma_0(R)\) the subgroup of \(M\) generated by \(R\). We denote by \(\mathscr{V}(R)\) the vector subspace of \(V\) generated by \(R\), that is to say \(\Gamma_0(R) \otimes \mathbb{Q}\). Applying these definitions to \(\mathscr{R}^*\), one constructs in the same way \(\Gamma_0(R^*)\), \(\mathscr{V}(R^*)\).

The reductive rank of \(\mathscr{R}\) is the number \[ \mathrm{rgred}(\mathscr{R}) = \mathrm{rang}(M) = \dim(V) = \dim(V^*) = \mathrm{rang}(M^*) = \mathrm{rgred}(\mathscr{R}^*). \] The semi-simple rank of \(\mathscr{R}\) is the number \[ \mathrm{rgss}(\mathscr{R}) = \mathrm{rang}(R) = \mathrm{rang}\,\Gamma_0(R)) = \dim(\mathscr{V}(R)). \] We shall see below that \(\mathrm{rgss}(\mathscr{R}) = \mathrm{rgss}(\mathscr{R}^*)\), that is to say that \(\mathscr{V}(R)\) and \(\mathscr{V}(R^*)\) have the same dimension.

We therefore have \(\mathrm{rgss}(\mathscr{R}) \leqslant \mathrm{rgred}(\mathscr{R})\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.1.7

We say that \(\mathscr{R}\) is semi-simple (resp. trivial) if \(\mathrm{rgss}(\mathscr{R}) = \mathrm{rgred}(\mathscr{R})\) (resp. \(\mathrm{rgss}(\mathscr{R}) = 0\)). For \(\mathscr{R}\) to be trivial it is therefore necessary and sufficient that \(R\) be empty. The trivial root datum of reductive rank zero is denoted \(0 = (\{0\}, \{0\}, \varnothing, \varnothing)\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.1.8

We denote by \(W(\mathscr{R})\) the group of transformations of \(M\) generated by the \(s_\alpha\), \(\alpha \in R\). It is called the Weyl group of \(\mathscr{R}\). We write \[ W^*(\mathscr{R}) = W(\mathscr{R}^*). \]

Then \(W(\mathscr{R})\) operates on \(R\), \(\Gamma_0(R)\), \(\mathscr{V}(R)\), \(M\) and \(V\). If \(w \in W(\mathscr{R})\) and \(x \in M\) (resp. \(x \in V\)), we have \(wx - x \in \Gamma_0(R)\) (resp. \(wx - x \in \mathscr{V}(R)\)); this is immediate from formula (1). The same holds for \(W^*(\mathscr{R})\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.1.9

For all \(\alpha \in R\), \(x \in V\), \(u \in V^*\), we have \[ (4)\qquad (s^*_\alpha(u), s_\alpha(x)) = (u, x). \]
Taking the scalar product of (1) and (1\(^*\)), one finds that the left-hand side is equal to \((u, x) + (u, \alpha)(\alpha^*, x)\big((\alpha^*, \alpha) - 2\big) = (u, x)\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 1.1.10

If one assumes \(0 \notin R\), \(0 \notin R^*\), then 1.1.9 is equivalent to (DR I).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.1.11

Let \(h \mapsto h^\vee\) denote the isomorphism of \(\mathrm{GL}(M)\) onto \(\mathrm{GL}(M^*)\) which associates to \(h\) its contragredient. Then formula (4) may also be written \[ (5)\qquad (s_\alpha)^\vee = s^*_\alpha. \]

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.1.12

The preceding isomorphism induces an isomorphism of \(W(\mathscr{R})\) onto \(W^*(\mathscr{R})\).

blocks.title: Scholium
blocks.html:
Scholium 1.1.13

By virtue of the preceding result, we shall identify \(W\) and \(W^*\), and we shall regard \(W\) as a group of transformations of \(R\), \(R^*\), \(M\), \(M^*\), \(\Gamma_0(R)\), \(\Gamma_0(R^*)\), \(V\), \(V^*\), \(\mathscr{V}(R)\), \(\mathscr{V}(R^*)\). We shall write \(s_\alpha\) for \(s^*_\alpha\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.2.1

Let \(p : M \to M^*\) (resp. \(V \to V^*\)) be the linear map defined by \[ (6)\qquad p(x) = \sum_{u \in R^*} (u, x)u. \]

Let us write \(\ell(x) = (p(x), x)\). We have the following properties: \[ (7)\qquad \ell(x) \geqslant 0, \qquad \ell(\alpha) > 0 \quad\text{for}\ \alpha \in R. \] \[ (8)\qquad \ell(w\,x) = \ell(x), \qquad\text{for}\ w \in W. \] \[ (9)\qquad (p(x), y) = (p(y), x), \qquad\text{for}\ x, y \in V. \] \[ (10)\qquad \ell(\alpha)\alpha^* = 2p(\alpha), \qquad\text{for}\ \alpha \in R. \]

The first three relations are immediate. Let us prove the last. By (1) we have, for \(u \in V^*\): \[ \begin{aligned} (u, \alpha)^2\,\alpha^* &= (u, \alpha)\,u - (u, \alpha)\,s_\alpha(u) \\ &= (u, \alpha)\,u + (u, s_\alpha(\alpha))\,s_\alpha(u) \\ &= (u, \alpha)\,u + (s_\alpha(u), \alpha)\,s_\alpha(u) \qquad (\text{since}\ s^2_\alpha = \mathrm{id}). \end{aligned} \] Since \(s_\alpha\) is a permutation of \(R^*\) (by (DR II)), it remains only to sum over \(u \in R^*\) to conclude.

blocks.title: Scholium
blocks.html:
Scholium 1.2.2

Relation (10) says that \(\alpha \mapsto \ell(\alpha)\alpha^*\) is the restriction to \(R\) of a linear map from \(M\) into \(M^*\). In particular, we have \[ (-\alpha)^* = -\alpha^*. \]

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.2.3

The map \(p\) induces an isomorphism of \(\mathscr{V}(R)\) onto \(\mathscr{V}(R)^*\).

Indeed, \(p\) maps \(\mathscr{V}(R)\) onto \(\mathscr{V}(R^*)\). We therefore have \[ \dim(\mathscr{V}(R)) \geqslant \dim(\mathscr{V}(R^*)). \] Applying this formula to the dual root datum, one deduces \[ \dim(\mathscr{V}(R)) = \dim(\mathscr{V}(R^*)), \] and \(p\), being surjective, is therefore also bijective.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.2.4

We have \(\dim(\mathscr{V}(R)) = \dim(\mathscr{V}(R^*))\), hence \[ \mathrm{rgss}(\mathscr{R}) = \mathrm{rgss}(\mathscr{R}^*). \]

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.2.5

The bilinear form \((u, x)\) is non-degenerate on \(\mathscr{V}(R^*) \times \mathscr{V}(R)\), and hence puts these \(\mathbb{Q}\)-vector spaces in duality.
Indeed, if \((u, x) = 0\) for all \(u \in R^*\), then \(p(x) = 0\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.2.6

The symmetric bilinear form \((p(x), y)\) is positive non-degenerate on \(\mathscr{V}(R)\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.2.7

\(W\) operates faithfully on \(R\) (and hence on the other sets of 1.1.13).

Indeed, let \(u \in V^*\). Let \(w \in W\); suppose that \(w(\alpha) = \alpha\) for \(\alpha \in R\) and let us prove that \(w(u) = u\). We have \[ (w(u) - u, \alpha) = (w(u), \alpha) - (u, \alpha) = (u, w^{-1}(\alpha)) - (u, \alpha) = 0. \] But \(w(u) - u \in \mathscr{V}(R^*)\). If it is orthogonal to all the roots, it is zero by 1.2.5.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.2.8

The group \(W\) is finite.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.2.9

The operations of \(W\) respect the correspondence between roots and coroots. In other words, for \(\alpha \in R\) and \(w \in W\), we have \[ w(\alpha^*) = w(\alpha)^*. \]

It suffices to verify this for \(w = s_\beta\), \(\beta \in R\), that is to say to verify the formula \[ s_\beta(\alpha^*) = s_\beta(\alpha)^*. \] Now we have successively \[ \begin{aligned} s_\beta(\alpha)^* &= 2\ell(s_\beta(\alpha))^{-1}\, p(s_\beta(\alpha)) \\ &= 2\ell(\alpha)^{-1} \sum_{u \in R^*} (u, s_\beta(\alpha))u \\ &= 2\ell(\alpha)^{-1} \sum_{u \in R^*} (s_\beta(u), s_\beta(\alpha))s_\beta(u) \\ &= 2\ell(\alpha)^{-1} \sum_{u \in R^*} (u, \alpha)\, s_\beta(u) \\ &= 2\ell(\alpha)^{-1} s_\beta(p(\alpha)) = s_\beta(\alpha^*). \end{aligned} \]

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.2.10

If \(\alpha \in R\) and \(w \in W\), we have \[ ws_\alpha w^{-1} = s_{w(\alpha)}. \]
Indeed, \[ \begin{aligned} ws_\alpha w^{-1}(x) &= x - (\alpha^*, w^{-1}(x))w(\alpha) \\ &= x - (w(\alpha^*), x)w(\alpha) \\ &= x - (w(\alpha)^*, x)w(\alpha) = s_{w(\alpha)}(x). \end{aligned} \]

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.2.11

Let \(R' \subset R\). For \((M, M^*, R', R'^*)\) to be a root datum, it is necessary and sufficient that \(\alpha, \beta \in R'\) imply \(s_\alpha(\beta) \in R'\).
2. Relations between two roots
2.1. Proportional roots

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.1.1

Let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be two roots. The following conditions are equivalent:

(i) There exists \(k \in \mathbb{Q}\) with \(\alpha = k\,\beta\).

(ii) \(s_\alpha = s_\beta\).

Moreover, under these conditions, we have \(\alpha^* = k^{-1}\,\beta^*\) and \(k\) is equal to one of the numbers \(1\), \(-1\), \(2\), \(-2\), \(1/2\), \(-1/2\).

Suppose first (i). We have first of all \[ \alpha^* = \ell(\alpha)^{-1}\,2\,p(\alpha) = k^{-2}\ell(\beta)^{-1}\,2\,k\,p(\beta) = k^{-1}\,\beta^*. \] This immediately implies \(s_\alpha = s_\beta\). Conversely, if \(s_\alpha = s_\beta\), then \[ \alpha = s_\alpha(-\alpha) = s_\beta(-\alpha) = (\beta^*, \alpha)\,\beta - \alpha, \] so that (ii) implies (i). Finally, if \(\alpha = k\,\beta\), then \[ (\alpha^*, \beta) = 2k^{-1}, \qquad (\beta^*, \alpha) = 2k, \] so that \(2k\) and \(2k^{-1}\) are integers, and we are done.

blocks.title: Application
blocks.html:
Application 2.1.2

The root data \(\mathscr{R}\) such that \(\mathrm{rgss}(\mathscr{R}) = 1\) are of one of the two following types:

(i) Type \(\mathrm{A}_1\): there exists an \(\alpha \in M\) such that the roots are \(\alpha\) and \(-\alpha\). The coroots are then \(\alpha^*\) and \(-\alpha^*\).

(ii) Type \(\mathrm{A}'_1\): there exists an \(\alpha \in M\) such that the roots are \(\alpha\), \(-\alpha\), \(2\alpha\), \(-2\alpha\). The coroots are then \(\alpha^*\), \(-\alpha^*\), \(\alpha^*/2\), \(-\alpha^*/2\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.1.3

We say that \(\alpha \in R\) is indivisible if \(\alpha/2 \notin R\). We say that \(\mathscr{R}\) is reduced if every root is indivisible.
For \(\mathscr{R}\) to be reduced it is necessary and sufficient that \(\mathscr{R}^*\) be so. If \(\alpha\) is indivisible and if \(w \in W\), then \(w(\alpha)\) is indivisible.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.1.4

Let \(\alpha \in R\). If \(\alpha\) is indivisible, we set \(\mathrm{ind}(\alpha) = \alpha\). Otherwise, we set \(\mathrm{ind}(\alpha) = \alpha/2\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.1.5

If \(\alpha \in R\) is indivisible and if \(k\,\alpha \in R\), where \(k \in \mathbb{Q}\), then \(k \in \mathbb{Z}\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.1.6

Let \(\mathscr{R}\) be a root datum. Then \[ \mathrm{ind}(\mathscr{R}) = (M, M^*, \mathrm{ind}(R), \mathrm{ind}(R)^*) \] is a reduced root datum, and one has \[ W(\mathrm{ind}(\mathscr{R})) = W(\mathscr{R}). \]
Indeed, \(\mathrm{ind}(\mathscr{R})\) is a root datum by 1.2.11, since the Weyl group permutes the indivisible roots. The second assertion follows from 2.1.1.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 2.1.7

One does not have \(\mathrm{ind}(R)^* = \mathrm{ind}(R^*)\), hence not \(\mathrm{ind}(\mathscr{R}^*) = \mathrm{ind}(\mathscr{R})^*\) either, if \(R\) is not reduced.
2.2. Orthogonal roots

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.2.1

Let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be two roots. We have \[ (11)\qquad \ell(\alpha)\,(\alpha^*, \beta) = \ell(\beta)\,(\beta^*, \alpha). \]
This follows at once from 1.2.1, formulas (9) and (10).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.2.2

The following conditions are equivalent:

(i) \((\alpha^*, \beta) = 0\), \(\qquad\) (i bis) \((\beta^*, \alpha) = 0\),

(ii) \((p(\alpha), \beta) = 0\),

(iii) \(s_\alpha(\beta) = \beta\), \(\qquad\) (iii bis) \(s_\beta(\alpha) = \alpha\),

(iv) \(s_\alpha(\beta^*) = \beta^*\), \(\qquad\) (iv bis) \(s_\beta(\alpha^*) = \alpha^*\),

(v) \(s_\alpha \ne s_\beta\) and \(s_\alpha\) and \(s_\beta\) commute.

All the equivalences are immediate except those involving (v). Let us show that (i) (and (i bis)) imply (v). We have \[ s_\alpha s_\beta(x) = x - (\beta^*, x)\,\beta - (\alpha^*, x)\,\alpha + (\beta^*, x)\,(\alpha^*, \beta)\,\alpha. \] If \((\alpha^*, \beta) = 0\), then \((\beta^*, \alpha) = 0\) and \(s_\alpha s_\beta(x) = s_\beta s_\alpha(x)\).

Suppose conversely (v). We then have \[ s_\alpha = s_\beta s_\alpha s_\beta = s_{s_\beta(\alpha)} \qquad (\text{by 1.2.10}). \] By 2.1, there exists \(k \in \mathbb{Q}^*\) such that \(\alpha = k\,s_\beta(\alpha) = k\,\alpha - k\,(\beta^*, \alpha)\,\beta\). Since \(s_\alpha \ne s_\beta\), \(\beta\) and \(\alpha\) are not proportional by 2.1.1, hence \((\beta^*, \alpha) = 0\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.2.3

Two roots satisfying the equivalent conditions of 2.2.2 are said to be orthogonal.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 2.2.4

The roots \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are orthogonal if and only if the coroots \(\alpha^*\) and \(\beta^*\) are orthogonal.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.2.5

If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are two orthogonal roots, then \(\alpha + \beta \in R\) if and only if \(\alpha - \beta \in R\).
Indeed \(s_\beta(\alpha + \beta) = s_\beta(\alpha) + s_\beta(\beta) = \alpha - \beta\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.2.6

Let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be two non-orthogonal roots. If one defines \(\ell(\gamma^*)\) for a coroot \(\gamma^*\) as \(\ell\) of the root \(\gamma^*\) of \(\mathscr{R}^*\), one has the relation \[ (12)\qquad \ell(\alpha)\ell(\alpha^*) = \ell(\beta)\ell(\beta^*). \]

Indeed, if one multiplies formula (11) by the corresponding formula for the transposed datum, one finds: \[ (\beta^*, \alpha)\,(\alpha^*, \beta)\,\ell(\alpha)\,\ell(\alpha^*) = (\beta^*, \alpha)\,(\alpha^*, \beta)\,\ell(\beta)\,\ell(\beta^*). \]
2.3. General case

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.3.1

If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are any two roots, we have \[ (13)\qquad 0 \leqslant (\alpha^*, \beta)(\beta^*, \alpha) \leqslant 4. \] If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are neither proportional nor orthogonal, we have \[ 1 \leqslant (\alpha^*, \beta)(\beta^*, \alpha) \leqslant 3. \]
Indeed, we have \(4\,(p(\alpha), \beta)^2 = \ell(\alpha)\ell(\beta)(\alpha^*, \beta)(\beta^*, \alpha)\), and the bilinear form \((p(x), y)\) is positive non-degenerate (1.2.6) on \(\mathscr{V}(R)\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.3.2

Let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be two non-orthogonal roots. If \(\ell(\alpha) = \ell(\beta)\), there exists \(w \in W\) with \(w(\alpha) = \beta\).

Indeed, if \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are proportional, we have \(\alpha = \beta\) or \(\alpha = -\beta\); in that case we take \(w = 1\) or \(w = s_\alpha\). If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are neither proportional nor orthogonal, we have \((\beta^*, \alpha) = (\alpha^*, \beta) = \pm 1\) (2.3.1 and formula (11)). If \((\beta^*, \alpha) = (\alpha^*, \beta) = 1\), we take \(w = s_\beta s_\alpha s_\beta\). If \((\beta^*, \alpha) = (\alpha^*, \beta) = -1\), we take \(w = s_\alpha s_\beta\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.3.3

If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are two roots, if \(\alpha \ne \beta\) and \((\beta^*, \alpha) > 0\) (resp. if \(\alpha \ne -\beta\) and \((\beta^*, \alpha) < 0\)), then \(\alpha - \beta\) (resp. \(\alpha + \beta\)) is a root.

The second case is deduced from the first by changing \(\beta\) into \(-\beta\). If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are proportional and if \((\beta^*, \alpha) > 0\), then we have \(\beta = \alpha\), \(2\beta = \alpha\) or \(\beta = 2\alpha\). The first case is excluded. In the others, we have respectively \(\alpha - \beta = \beta \in R\) or \(\alpha - \beta = -\alpha \in R\). If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are not proportional, \((\alpha^*, \beta)\) and \((\beta^*, \alpha)\) are two strictly positive integers whose product is at most 3. One of them is therefore equal to 1. If \((\beta^*, \alpha) = 1\), we have \(\alpha - \beta = s_\beta(\alpha) \in R\); if \((\alpha^*, \beta) = 1\), we have \(\alpha - \beta = -s_\alpha(\beta) \in R\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.3.4

Let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be two non-proportional roots. If \(\beta - \alpha\) is not a root, then \(\beta + k\,\alpha \in R\) for \(k = -(\alpha^*, \beta)\), but not for \(k = -(\alpha^*, \beta) + 1\).
Indeed, we have \(s_\alpha(\beta) = \beta - (\alpha^*, \beta)\,\alpha\), \[ s_\alpha(\beta - \alpha) = \beta + (-(\alpha^*, \beta) + 1)\alpha. \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.3.5

Let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be two non-proportional roots. The set of integers \(k\) such that \(\beta + k\,\alpha \in R\) is an interval \([p, q]\) (\(p \leqslant 0\), \(q \geqslant 0\)), and one has \(p + q = -(\alpha^*, \beta)\).

To prove the first assertion, it suffices for instance to prove that if \(\beta + k\,\alpha \in R\), \(k\) an integer \(> 0\), then \(\beta + (k - 1)\,\alpha \in R\). If \(k = 1\), this is trivial. If \(k \geqslant 2\), we have \[ (\alpha^*, \beta + k\,\alpha) = (\alpha^*, \beta) + 2k \geqslant -3 + 4 > 0, \] and one concludes by 2.3.3. Let then \([p, q]\) be the interval in question. Applying 2.3.4 to \(\beta + p\,\alpha\), one finds \[ q - p = -(\alpha^*, \beta + p\,\alpha) = -(\alpha^*, \beta) + 2p. \]

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 2.3.6

The preceding formula contains the qualitative statements 2.2.5 and 2.3.3.
3. Simple roots, positive roots
3.1. Systems of simple roots

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.1.1

Let \(\alpha\) and \(\alpha_i\), \(i = 1, \ldots, n\), be roots. Suppose \(\alpha\) distinct from the \(\alpha_i\). If we have a relation \[ \alpha = \sum_{i=1}^{n} q_i\,\alpha_i, \qquad q_i \in \mathbb{Q}_+, \] there exists an \(i\) with \(q_i \ne 0\), \((\alpha^*, \alpha_i) > 0\), \(\alpha - \alpha_i \in R\).
Indeed, one writes \(2 = (\alpha^*, \alpha) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} q_i\,(\alpha^*, \alpha_i)\), which proves the first two assertions. The third then follows from 2.3.3.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.1.2

Let \(\alpha\) and \(\alpha_i\), \(i = 1, \ldots, n\), be roots. If \[ \alpha = \sum_{i=1}^{n} m_i\,\alpha_i, \qquad m_i \in \mathbb{N}_+, \] there exists a sequence \(\beta_1, \ldots, \beta_m\) of roots taken from among the \(\alpha_i\) (not necessarily pairwise distinct) such that, if one writes \[ \gamma_p = \sum_{i=1}^{p} \beta_i, \qquad p = 1, \ldots, m, \] one has \(\gamma_p \in R\) and \(\gamma_m = \alpha\).

Let us argue by induction on the integer \(\sum m_i = m'\). If \(\alpha\) is equal to one of the \(\alpha_i\), say \(\alpha_{i_0}\) (which is automatic if \(m' = 1\)), we take \(m = 1\), \(\beta_1 = \alpha_{i_0}\). Otherwise, we apply the preceding lemma, and there exists an \(i\) such that \(m_i \ne 0\) and \(\alpha - \alpha_i\) is a root. We then have \((m_i - 1) \in \mathbb{N}\) and \[ \alpha - \alpha_i = (m_i - 1)\,\alpha_i + \sum_{j \ne i} m_j\,\alpha_j. \] It remains only to apply the induction hypothesis to \(\alpha - \alpha_i\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.1.3

Let \(R' \subset R\). The following conditions are equivalent:

(i) If \(\alpha, \beta \in R'\) and \(\alpha + \beta \in R\), then \(\alpha + \beta \in R'\).

(ii) \((\mathbb{N} \cdot R') \cap R \subset R'\).
Indeed, one clearly has (ii)\(\Rightarrow\)(i). The converse follows at once from the proposition.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.1.4

A set of roots satisfying the conditions of 3.1.3 is said to be closed.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.1.5

Let \(\Delta \subset R\) be a set of roots. The following conditions are equivalent:

(i) The elements of \(\Delta\) are indivisible, linearly independent, and \[ R \subset (\mathbb{Q}_+ \cdot \Delta) \cup (-\mathbb{Q}_+ \cdot \Delta). \]

(ii) The elements of \(\Delta\) are linearly independent and \[ R \subset (\mathbb{N} \cdot \Delta) \cup (-\mathbb{N} \cdot \Delta). \]

(iii) Every root can be written in a unique way as a linear combination, with integer coefficients all of the same sign, of the elements of \(\Delta\).

Obviously (ii) \(\Leftrightarrow\) (iii). Let us prove (iii) \(\Rightarrow\) (i). It suffices to show that (iii) implies that the elements of \(\Delta\) are indivisible. So let \(\beta \in \Delta\) be divisible. We have \(\beta/2 \in R\), whence \[ \frac{\beta}{2} = \sum m_i \alpha_i, \quad m_i \in \mathbb{Z}, \alpha_i \in \Delta; \] but we also have \(\beta/2 = (1/2)\beta\), which contradicts the fact that the elements of \(\Delta\) are linearly independent (over \(\mathbb{Q}\)). Let us prove (i) \(\Rightarrow\) (ii). Let \(\alpha \in R\). Denote by \(\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \cdots \alpha_n\) the (distinct) elements of \(\Delta\). We thus have a unique expression \[ \varepsilon\,\alpha = \sum q_i \alpha_i \qquad q_i \in \mathbb{Q}_+,\ \varepsilon = \pm 1. \] Let us show that the \(q_i\) are integers. This is certainly true if they are all zero except one (cf. 2.1.5). Otherwise, \(\alpha\) is distinct from the \(\alpha_i\), and applying 3.1.1 one finds an \(i_0\) such that \(\alpha' = \varepsilon\alpha - \alpha_{i_0} \in R\) and \(q_{i_0} \ne 0\). This gives \[ \alpha' = (q_{i_0} - 1)\,\alpha_{i_0} + \sum_{i \ne i_0} q_i\,\alpha_i. \] Since at least one of the \(q_i\), \(i \ne i_0\), is non-zero, (i) implies that \(q_{i_0} - 1 > 0\). One repeats the operation for \(\alpha'\), and after a finite number of steps one has proved that the \(q_i\) are integers.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.1.6

A set \(\Delta\) of roots satisfying the conditions of 3.1.5 is called a system of simple roots, or a base of \(R\).
If \(w \in W\) and if \(\Delta\) is a system of simple roots, then \(w(\Delta)\) is a system of simple roots.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.1.7

This definition involves only \(R\) and not \(\mathscr{R}\); in fact it involves only \(\mathrm{ind}(R)\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.1.8

If \(\Delta\) is a system of simple roots, \(\Delta\) is a basis of the free abelian group \(\Gamma_0(R)\). We therefore have \(\mathrm{Card}(\Delta) = \mathrm{rgss}(\mathscr{R})\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.1.9

The conditions of 3.1.5 are then obviously equivalent to the following:

(i′) The elements of \(\Delta\) are indivisible, are \(\leqslant \mathrm{rgss}(R)\) in number, and \(R \subset (\mathbb{Q}_+ \cdot \Delta) \cup (-\mathbb{Q}_+ \cdot \Delta)\).

(ii′) One has \(\mathrm{Card}(\Delta) \leqslant \mathrm{rgss}(R)\) and \(R \subset (\mathbb{N} \cdot \Delta) \cup (-\mathbb{N} \cdot \Delta)\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.1.10

If \(\Delta\) is a system of simple roots, then \(\mathrm{ind}(\Delta^*)\) is a system of simple coroots (i.e. a system of simple roots of \(R^*\)).
Indeed, if \[ \alpha = \sum a_i\,\alpha_i \] \[ \alpha^* = \sum a_i \frac{\ell(a_i)}{\ell(\alpha)} \alpha^*_i, \] which proves that \(\mathrm{ind}(\Delta^*)\) satisfies (i′). Moreover

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.1.11

If \(\Delta\) is a system of simple roots and if \[ \beta = \sum_{\alpha \in \Delta} a_\alpha\,\alpha, \qquad a_\alpha \in \mathbb{Z} \] is the expression of \(\beta\) with respect to \(\Delta\), then \(4\,a_\alpha\ell(\alpha)\) is divisible by \(\ell(\beta)\) (and even by \(4\,\ell(\beta)\) if \(\alpha\) is indivisible).
Before going on to state further properties of systems of simple roots, let us show that they exist.
3.2. Systems of positive roots

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.2.1

A set \(R_+ \subset R\) is called a system of positive roots of \(\mathscr{R}\) if it satisfies the following conditions:

(P 1) \(R_+ \cap -R_+ = \varnothing\).

(P 2) \(R_+ \cup -R_+ = R\).

(P 3) \((\mathbb{Q}_+ \cdot R_+) \cap R \subset R_+\).

In particular, such a set is closed. We shall see later that in fact a closed set satisfying (P 1) and (P 2) also satisfies (P 3), hence is a system of positive roots. If \(w \in W\) and if \(R_+\) is a system of positive roots, then \(w(R_+)\) is a system of positive roots.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.2.2

This definition involves only \(R\). We shall also say that \(R_+\) is a system of positive roots of \(R\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.2.3

From (P 1) and (P 2) one immediately obtains \[ \mathrm{Card}(R_+) = \mathrm{Card}(R)/2. \] It follows that if \(R_+\) and \(R'_+\) are two systems of positive roots and if \(R_+ \subset R'_+\), then \(R_+ = R'_+\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.2.4

If \(R_+\) is a system of positive roots, \(R^*_+\) is a system of positive coroots (i.e. a system of positive roots of \(R^*\)).
This follows immediately from 1.1.4 and 1.2.2.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.2.5

Let \(\Delta\) be a system of simple roots. One sets \[ \mathscr{P}(\Delta) = (\mathbb{Q}_+ \cdot \Delta) \cap R = (\mathbb{N}_+ \cdot \Delta) \cap R. \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.2.6

If \(\Delta\) is a system of simple roots, \(\mathscr{P}(\Delta)\) is a system of positive roots. If \(\Delta\) is a system of simple roots and \(R_+\) a system of positive roots, one has the equivalence: \[ \Delta \subset R_+ \iff R_+ = \mathscr{P}(\Delta). \]
The first assertion is immediate. If \(\Delta \subset R_+\), then \(\mathscr{P}(\Delta) \subset R_+\) by (P 3), hence \(\mathscr{P}(\Delta) = R_+\) by 3.2.3. The rest is trivial.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.2.7

Systems of positive roots exist: let \(\geqslant\) be a structure of totally ordered vector space on \(\mathscr{V}(R)\). The set of roots \(\geqslant 0\) for this order relation is a system of positive roots.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 3.2.8

Let \(R_+\) be a system of positive roots. There exists a unique system of simple roots \(\mathscr{S}(R_+)\) such that \(\mathscr{S}(R_+) \subset R_+\), i.e. \(R_+ = \mathscr{P}(\mathscr{S}(R_+))\).
Uniqueness follows immediately from:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.2.9

Let \(\Delta\) be a system of simple roots. Then for \(\alpha \in \mathscr{P}(\Delta)\) to belong to \(\Delta\), it is necessary and sufficient that \(\alpha\) not be the sum of two elements of \(\mathscr{P}(\Delta)\).
This lemma follows immediately from the definitions and from 3.1.2.

Let us now prove the existence of \(\mathscr{S}(R_+)\). Consider the set of subsets \(T\) of \(R_+\) such that \(T = \mathrm{ind}(T)\) and \((\mathbb{Q}_+ \cdot T) \supset R_+\). This set is non-empty, for it contains \(\mathrm{ind}(R_+)\). Let \(\Delta\) be a minimal element of this set for the inclusion relation. Let us show that \(\Delta\) is a system of simple roots, that is to say, by 3.1.5 (i), that \(\Delta\) is a free subset of \(M\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.2.10

If \(\alpha, \beta \in \Delta\), \(m, n \in \mathbb{Q}\) and \(m\alpha + n\beta \in R\), then \(mn \geqslant 0\).

If \(mn < 0\), one may write (after possibly interchanging \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\)) \[ a\alpha - b\beta \in R_+,\ a, b \in \mathbb{Q}_+,\ a \cdot b \ne 0, \] hence there exists by hypothesis a relation \[ a\alpha - b\beta = \sum_{\gamma \in \Delta} c(\gamma)\gamma, \qquad c(\gamma) \in \mathbb{Q}_+. \]

If \(a \leqslant c(\alpha)\), it is written \[ -\beta = b^{-1}(c(\alpha) - a)\alpha + \sum_{\gamma \in \Delta\, \gamma \ne \alpha} b^{-1}c(\gamma)\gamma \in \mathbb{Q}_+ \cdot R_+ \cap R, \] which, by (P 3) and (P 1), gives \(\beta \in R_+ \cap -R_+ = \varnothing\).

If, on the contrary, \(a > c(\alpha)\), one writes \[ \alpha = (a - c(\alpha)^{-1})b\beta + \sum_{\gamma \in \Delta\, \gamma \ne \alpha} (a - c(\alpha))^{-1}c(\gamma)\gamma, \] which proves that \(\Delta \subset \mathbb{Q}_+ \cdot (\Delta - \{\alpha\})\), contrary to the minimality of \(\Delta\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.2.11

If \(\alpha, \beta \in \Delta\), then \((\beta^*, \alpha) \leqslant 0\).
Indeed, \(s_\beta(\alpha) = \alpha - (\beta^*, \alpha)\,\beta \in R\), and one concludes by 3.2.10.

Let us now prove that \(\Delta\) is free. If one has a linear relation between elements of \(\Delta\), one may suppose it written in the form \[ x = \sum_{\alpha \in \mathrm{I}} m_\alpha \alpha = \sum_{\beta \in \mathrm{J}} n_\beta \beta \] with \(\mathrm{I} \subset \Delta\); \(\mathrm{J} \subset \Delta\); \(\mathrm{I} \cap \mathrm{J} = \varnothing\); \(\mathrm{I} \ne \varnothing\); \(m_\alpha, n_\beta \in \mathbb{Q}_+\). One then has \[ 2p(x) = \sum_{\beta \in \mathrm{J}} n_\beta \ell(\beta)\beta^*, \] hence \[ 0 \leqslant 2(p(x), x) = \sum_{\alpha \in \mathrm{I}\, \beta \in \mathrm{J}} m_\alpha n_\beta \ell(\beta)(\beta^*, \alpha) \leqslant 0. \] By 1.2.6 this entails \(x = 0\), hence a non-trivial relation. \[ \sum_{\alpha \in \Delta} m(\alpha)\alpha = 0, \qquad m(\alpha) \in \mathbb{Q}_+. \]
If \(m(\alpha_0) \ne 0\), one has \(-\alpha_0 \in \mathbb{Q}_+ \cdot R_+ \cap -R_+ = \varnothing\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.2.12

One has the relations \[ \Delta \subset R_+ \iff R_+ = \mathscr{P}(\Delta) \iff \Delta = \mathscr{S}(R_+) \] \[ \mathscr{P}(\mathrm{ind}(\Delta^*)) = \mathscr{P}(\Delta)^*, \qquad \mathscr{S}(R^*_+) = \mathrm{ind}(\mathscr{S}(R_+)^*); \] \[ \mathscr{S}(w(R_+)) = w(\mathscr{S}(R_+)), \qquad \mathscr{P}(w(\Delta)) = w(\mathscr{P}(\Delta)). \]

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.2.13

If one has chosen a system of simple roots \(\Delta\), the elements of \(\mathscr{P}(\Delta)\) will be called positive. If one has chosen a system of positive roots \(R_+\), the elements of \(\mathscr{S}(R_+)\) will be called simple.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.2.14

Let \(R_+\) be a system of positive roots. Let \(\alpha \in R_+\). The following conditions are equivalent:

(i) \(\alpha\) is simple (i.e. \(\alpha \in \mathscr{S}(R_+)\)).

(ii) \(\alpha\) is not the sum of two elements of \(R_+\).

(iii) \(R_+ - \{\alpha\}\) is closed.
The equivalence of (i) and (ii) follows immediately from 3.2.9. The equivalence of (ii) and (iii) is immediate.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.2.15

Let \(\Delta\) be a system of simple roots. The sum of the coefficients of the decomposition of a root \(\alpha\) along \(\Delta\) is called the order of \(\alpha\) relative to \(\Delta\) and is denoted \(\mathrm{ord}_\Delta(\alpha)\).
One has the equivalences: \[ \alpha \in \mathscr{P}(\Delta) \iff \mathrm{ord}_\Delta(\alpha) > 0, \qquad \alpha \in \Delta \iff \mathrm{ord}_\Delta(\alpha) = 1. \]

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.2.16

Let \(\Delta\) be a system of simple roots. Let \(\alpha \in R_+\). There exists a sequence \(\alpha_i \in \Delta\), \(i = 1, 2, \ldots, m\), with \[ \alpha_1 + \alpha_2 + \cdots + \alpha_p \in \mathscr{P}(\Delta) \quad\text{for}\quad p = 1, \ldots m, \] \[ \alpha_1 + \alpha_2 + \cdots + \alpha_m = \alpha. \] Moreover, for every sequence \(\alpha_i\) satisfying these conditions, one has \(m = \mathrm{ord}_\Delta(\alpha)\).
Trivial by 3.1.2.
3.3. Characterisation and conjugacy of systems of positive roots

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.3.1

If \(\alpha \in \mathscr{P}(\Delta)\), \(\beta \in \Delta\) and if \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are not proportional, then \(s_\beta(\alpha) \in \mathscr{P}(\Delta)\).

Indeed, \(s_\beta(\alpha) = \alpha - (\beta^*, \alpha)\,\beta\). Since there is at least one simple root other than \(\beta\) which occurs in the decomposition of \(\alpha\) with a non-zero (hence strictly positive) coefficient, and so also in the decomposition of \(s_\beta(\alpha)\) with the same coefficient, \(s_\beta(\alpha)\) is positive as well.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.3.2

If \(\beta \in \Delta\), the symmetry \(s_\beta\) permutes the elements of \(\mathscr{P}(\Delta)\) not proportional to \(\beta\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.3.3

If \(\alpha \in \mathscr{P}(\Delta)\), \(\alpha \notin \Delta\), \(\alpha\) indivisible, there exists a \(\beta \in \Delta\) with \(s_\beta(\alpha) \in \mathscr{P}(\Delta)\), \(\mathrm{ord}_\Delta(s_\beta(\alpha)) < \mathrm{ord}_\Delta(\alpha)\).
Indeed, there exists by 3.1.1 a \(\beta \in \Delta\) with \((\beta^*, \alpha) > 0\). Since \(\alpha\) is indivisible and \(\notin \Delta\), it cannot be proportional to \(\beta\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.3.4

If \(\alpha \in \mathscr{P}(\Delta)\) is indivisible, there exists a sequence \(\beta_p\), \(p = 1, 2, \ldots q\), \(\beta_p \in \Delta\) with \[ \alpha_p = s_{\beta_1} s_{\beta_2} \cdots s_{\beta_p}(\alpha) \in \mathscr{P}(\Delta), \qquad p = 1, \ldots q, \] and \(\alpha_q \in \Delta\).
This follows from 3.3.3 by induction on \(\mathrm{ord}_\Delta(\alpha)\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.3.5

The Weyl group is generated by the \(s_\alpha\), \(\alpha \in \Delta\). Every indivisible root is conjugate to a simple root under an element of the Weyl group.
The second assertion follows immediately from 3.3.4. The first follows from it by 1.2.10 and 2.1.1.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.3.6

Let \(R_+\) be a system of positive roots. Let \(P' \subset R\) satisfy (P 2) and be closed. Then there exists a \(w \in W\) such that \(w(R_+) \subset P'\).
Let us state the corollaries at once.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.3.7

The Weyl group acts transitively on the set of systems of positive roots (resp. of systems of simple roots).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.3.8

For a subset \(P\) of \(R\) to be a system of positive roots, it is necessary and sufficient that it satisfy (P 1) and (P 2) and be closed.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.3.9

If one endows \(\Gamma_0(R)\) with a structure of ordered group such that every root is \(> 0\) or \(< 0\), the set of roots positive for this order structure is a system of positive roots.

Let us now prove 3.3.6. One can find a \(w \in W\) such that \(\mathrm{Card}(w(R_+) \cap P')\) is maximal, hence, replacing \(R_+\) by \(w(R_+)\), assume that \[ \mathrm{Card}(R_+ \cap P') \geqslant \mathrm{Card}(R_+ \cap s_\alpha(P')) \] for all \(\alpha \in \mathscr{S}(R_+) = \Delta\). Let us prove that \(R_+ \subset P'\). Otherwise, \(P'\) being closed, there exists \(\alpha \in \Delta\), \(\alpha \notin P'\). But since \(P'\) satisfies (P 2), one then has \(-\alpha \in P'\) (hence \(-2\alpha \in P'\) if \(2\alpha\) is a root). For every \(\beta \in R_+ \cap P'\), one has \(\beta \ne \alpha\); if \(2\alpha\) is not a root, one then has \(s_\alpha(\beta) \in R_+\) (by 3.3.1), hence \[ s_\alpha(R_+ \cap P') \subset R_+ \cap s_\alpha(P'); \] but \(R_+ \cap s_\alpha(P')\) also contains \(\alpha = s_\alpha(-\alpha)\), which contradicts the assumed inequality. If \(2\alpha\) is a root, one argues in the same way.
In order to study the sets of roots satisfying (P 2) and closed, we are thus reduced to the case where they contain the set of positive roots.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.3.10

Let \(R_+\) be a system of positive roots. Let \(P'\) be closed, \(R_+ \subset P' \subset R\). If one puts \(T = \mathscr{S}(R_+) \cap -P'\), then \(P'\) is the union of \(R_+\) and of the set of roots which are linear combinations with negative coefficients of the elements of \(T\).

Let us prove the assertion by induction on the order of a root \(u \in P' - R_+\). Put \(\Delta = \mathscr{S}(R_+)\). If \(\mathrm{ord}_\Delta(u) = -1\), then \(-u \in \mathscr{S}(R_+)\) and \(u \in -T\). If \(\mathrm{ord}_\Delta(u) > -1\), there exists \(s \in \mathscr{S}(R_+)\) such that \(u + s \in R\) and \(\mathrm{ord}_\Delta(u + s) > \mathrm{ord}_\Delta(u)\) (one applies 3.1.4 to \(-u\)). Since \(u + s\) is the sum of two roots of \(P'\), it is an element of \(P'\), hence by the induction hypothesis a linear combination of the elements of \(T\). It suffices to check that \(s \in -P'\). Now \(-s = u - (u + s)\), but \(u \in P'\) and \(-(u + s)\) is positive, hence belongs to \(P'\).

blocks.title: Scholium
blocks.html:
Scholium 3.3.11

Let \(P'\) be a set of roots satisfying (P 2) and closed. There exists a system of simple roots \(\Delta\), and a subset \(T\) of \(\Delta\), such that \[ P' = [\mathbb{N} \cdot \Delta \cup -\mathbb{N} \cdot T] \cap R. \] If one writes \(R(T) = \mathbb{Z} \cdot T \cap R\), which is a closed and symmetric subset of \(R\), \(P'\) is thus the disjoint union of \(R(T)\) and of the closed subset of \(\mathscr{P}(\Delta)\) consisting of the \(\alpha \in \mathscr{P}(\Delta)\), \(\alpha \notin \mathbb{N} \cdot T\), i.e. of the positive roots which in their decomposition along \(\Delta\) "contain at least one root of \(\Delta - T\)".
3.4. Closed and symmetric sets of roots

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.4.1

Let \(R' \subset R\) be a set of roots of the root datum \(\mathscr{R}\). Suppose \(R'\) closed and symmetric (i.e. \(R' = -R'\)). Then \((M, M^*, R', R'^*)\) is a root datum; for every system of positive roots \(R_+\) of \(R\), \(R'_+ = R_+ \cap R'\) is a system of positive roots of \(R'\); the Weyl group \(W_{R'}\) of \((M, M^*, R', R'^*)\) is the subgroup of \(W(\mathscr{R})\) generated by the \(s_\alpha\), \(\alpha \in R'\).
The first assertion is trivial by 1.2.11, the second follows from 3.3.8, the third is obvious.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.4.2

Let \(w \in W_{R}\), The order of \(w\) is the smallest integer \(> 0\) \(n\) such that \(w^n(\alpha') = \alpha'\) for all \(\alpha' \in R'\).
It suffices to apply 1.2.7 to the root datum \((M, M^*, R', R'^*)\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.4.3

Let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be two non-proportional roots. Let \(n\) be the smallest positive integer such that \((s_\alpha s_\beta)^n(\alpha) = \alpha\) and \((s_\alpha s_\beta)^n(\beta) = \beta\). Then the subgroup \(W_{\alpha,\beta}\) of \(W\) generated by \(s_\alpha\) and \(s_\beta\) is defined by the relations: \[ s^2_\alpha = 1, \qquad s^2_\beta = 1, \qquad (s_\alpha s_\beta)^n = 1. \]
Taking 3.4.2 into account, it suffices to check:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.4.4

Let \(G\) be the group generated by two elements \(x\) and \(y\) subject to the relations \(x^2 = y^2 = 1\). Every normal subgroup of \(G\) containing neither \(x\) nor \(y\) is generated (as a normal subgroup) by an element of the form \((xy)^n\).
Indeed, an arbitrary element of \(G\) is written \((xy)^n\), or \(y(xy)^n\), or \((xy)^n x\), \(n\) an integer \(\geqslant 0\). Now the second element is conjugate to \(x\), the third to \(y\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.4.5

One computes the integer \(n\) immediately: if one puts \[ (\alpha^*, \beta) = p, \qquad (\beta^*, \alpha) = q, \] one has \[ (s_\alpha s_\beta)(\alpha) = (pq - 1)\,\alpha - q\,\beta, \qquad (s_\alpha s_\beta)(\beta) = p\,\alpha - \beta. \] The integer \(n\) is therefore the order of the matrix \[ \begin{pmatrix} pq - 1 & p \\ -q & -1 \end{pmatrix}. \]
One finds \[ \begin{aligned} pq = 0 &\Longrightarrow n = 2, \\ pq = 1 &\Longrightarrow n = 3, \\ pq = 2 &\Longrightarrow n = 4, \\ pq = 3 &\Longrightarrow n = 6. \end{aligned} \]
N. B. On writing that the order of the preceding matrix is finite, one recovers inequality (13).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.4.6

Let \(\Delta\) be a system of simple roots and \(\Delta' \subset \Delta\). One writes \[ R_{\Delta'} = R \cap (\mathbb{Q} \cdot S') = R \cap (\mathbb{Z} \cdot \Delta'). \]

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.4.7

\(R_{\Delta'}\) is closed and symmetric, \(\Delta'\) is a system of simple roots of the root datum \((M, M^*, R_{\Delta'}, R^*_{\Delta'})\), whose Weyl group is the subgroup \(W_{\Delta'}\) of \(W\) generated by the \(s_\alpha\), for \(\alpha \in \Delta'\). One has \(\Delta \cap R' = \Delta'\).
Trivial.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.4.8

Let \(R' \subset R\). The following conditions are equivalent:

(i) There exists a vector subspace \(V'\) of \(V\) (or of \(\mathscr{V}(R)\)) such that \(R' = R \cap V'\).

(ii) There exist a system of simple roots \(\Delta\) of \(R\) and a subset \(\Delta'\) of \(\Delta\) such that \(R' = R_{\Delta'}\).

More precisely, under these conditions, every system of simple roots \(\Delta'\) of \((M, M^*, R', R'^*)\) is contained in a system of simple roots \(\Delta\) of \(R\) and \(R' = R_{\Delta'}\).

One obviously has (ii) \(\Rightarrow\) (i). Suppose (i) is satisfied: then \(R'\) is closed and symmetric, hence \((M, M^*, R', R'^*)\) is a root datum. Let \(\Delta'\) be a system of simple roots of this datum and \(R'_+ = \mathscr{P}(\Delta')\). If \(V' = V\), then \(\Delta'\) is a system of simple roots of \(R\) and we are done. Otherwise, there exists an \(x \in V^*\) with \[ (x, V') = \{0\}, \qquad (x, \alpha) \ne 0 \quad\text{for all}\ \alpha \in R - R'. \] Let \(P_0 = \{\alpha \in R \mid (x, \alpha) > 0\}\). Put \(P = P_0 \cup P'\). For an \(\alpha \in R\), one has the equivalences \[ \begin{aligned} (x, \alpha) > 0 &\iff \alpha \in P_0, \\ (x, \alpha) < 0 &\iff \alpha \in -P_0, \\ (x, \alpha) = 0 &\iff \alpha \in R'. \end{aligned} \] It follows immediately from 3.3.8 that \(P\) is a system of positive roots of \(R\). Put \(S = \mathscr{S}(P)\). It obviously suffices to prove \(S' \subset S\). Otherwise let \(\alpha \in S'\), \(\alpha \notin S\). Then, by 3.2.14, there exist \(\beta, \gamma \in P\) with \(\alpha = \beta + \gamma\). If \(\beta, \gamma \in P_0\), one has \(\alpha \in P_0\), which is absurd. If \(\beta\) or \(\gamma\), say \(\beta\), belongs to \(P'\), then \(\gamma = \alpha - \beta \in R' \cap P = P'\); but then \(\alpha\) is not simple in \(P'\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.4.9

Under the preceding conditions, let \(\alpha \in \mathscr{P}(\Delta)\), \(\alpha \notin R'\). For every \(w \in W_{\Delta'}\), one has \(w(\alpha) \in \mathscr{P}(\Delta)\), \(w(\alpha) \notin R'\).
It suffices in fact to check it for \(w = s_\beta\), \(\beta \in \Delta'\), in which case it is trivial (3.3.1).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.4.10

Under the preceding conditions, the following conditions on a \(w \in W\) are equivalent:

(i) \(w \in W_\Delta\).

(ii) For every \(m \in M\), \(w(m) - m \in V'\).

(iii) For every \(\alpha \in R\), \(w(\alpha) - \alpha \in V'\).

One obviously has (i) \(\Rightarrow\) (ii) \(\Rightarrow\) (iii). Let us prove (iii) \(\Rightarrow\) (i). So let \(w \in W\), \(w \notin W_\Delta\), \(w(\alpha) - \alpha \in V'\) for all \(\alpha \in R\). Let us write \(w\) as a product of symmetries \(s_{\alpha_0} s_{\alpha_1} \ldots s_{\alpha_n}\), with \(\alpha_i \in \Delta\). After possibly replacing \(w\) by a partial product of the \(s_{\alpha_i}\), one may assume that \(w' = s_{\alpha_1} \ldots s_{\alpha_n} \in W_{\Delta'}\). One then has \[ w(\alpha) - r = w'(\alpha) - r - (w'^{-1}(\alpha^*_0), \alpha)\alpha_0. \] Taking \(\alpha = w'^{-1}(\alpha_0)\), one finds \(2\alpha_0 \in V'\), hence \(\alpha_0 \in \Delta'\), hence finally \(w = s_{\alpha_0} w' \in W_\Delta\), contrary to the hypothesis.
3.5. Miscellaneous remarks

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.5.1

Let \(R_+\) be a system of positive roots. Let us write \[ \rho_{R_+} = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{\alpha \in \mathrm{ind}(R_+)} \alpha. \] Then \((\beta^*, \rho_{R_+}) = 1\) for all \(\beta \in \mathscr{S}(R_+)\).
Indeed, one may write \[ 2\rho_{R_+} = \beta + \sum_{\substack{\alpha \in \mathrm{ind}(R_+) \\ \alpha \ne \beta}} \alpha, \] hence \(s_\beta(2\rho_{R_+}) = 2\rho_{R_+} - 2\beta\), by 3.3.2.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.5.2

Put \(\rho^*_{R_+} = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha^* \in \mathrm{ind}(R^*_+)} \alpha^*\). Then:

(i) \((\rho^*_{R_+}, \alpha) > 0\) for all \(\alpha \in R_+\) (i.e. \(\rho^*_{R_+} \in \mathscr{C}(R_+)\), cf. 3.6.8).

(ii) For all \(\alpha \in R\), one has \(\mathrm{ord}_{\mathscr{S}(R_+)}(\alpha) = (\rho^*_{R_+}, \alpha)\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.5.3

If \(w \in W\), one has \(\rho_{w(R_+)} = w(\rho_{R_+})\) and \(\rho^*_{w(R_+)} = w(\rho^*_{R_+})\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.5.4

Let \(\alpha\) and \(\gamma\) be two non-proportional roots, \(\alpha\) being assumed indivisible. There exist a system of simple roots containing \(\alpha\) and a root \(\beta\) such that \(\gamma = a\alpha + b\beta\), with \(a, b \in \mathbb{N}\).

Indeed, let us construct a basis of the vector space \(\mathscr{V}(R)\) containing \(\alpha_1 = \alpha\), \(\alpha_2 = \gamma\). Consider the lexicographic order relative to this basis. The set of roots \(> 0\) being denoted \(R_+\), it is clear that \(R_+\) is a system of positive roots and that the two smallest elements of \(R_+\) are simple. Now the smallest is \(\alpha\), the next is of the form \[ \beta = a\alpha + b\gamma, \qquad 0 < b \leqslant 1. \]
One thus has \(\gamma = b^{-1}\beta - b^{-1}a\alpha\) and \(b^{-1} > 0\), hence also \(-b^{-1}a > 0\).
Let us finally make two remarks on the group \(\Gamma_0(R)\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.5.5

Let \(G\) be an abelian group and \(f : R \to G\) a map satisfying the following two conditions:

(i) If \(\alpha \in R\), \(f(-\alpha) = -f(\alpha)\).

(ii) If \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), \(\alpha + \beta \in R\), \(f(\alpha + \beta) = f(\alpha) + f(\beta)\).

Then there exists a unique group homomorphism \(\overline{f} : \Gamma_0(R) \to G\) such that \(\overline{f}(\alpha) = f(\alpha)\) for \(\alpha \in R\).

Indeed, if \(\Delta\) is a system of simple roots of \(R\), and if \(\beta \in R\) is written \(\sum_{\alpha \in \Delta} a(\alpha)\alpha\), it follows immediately from 3.2.16 that \(f(\beta) = \sum_{\alpha \in \Delta} a(\alpha)f(\alpha)\). Now \(\Delta\) is a basis of \(\Gamma_0(R)\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.5.6

Let \(\Delta\) be a system of simple roots. There exists on \(\Gamma_0(R)\) a structure of totally ordered group such that the roots \(> 0\) are the elements of \(\mathscr{P}(\Delta)\) and such that \(\alpha \mapsto \mathrm{ord}_\Delta(\alpha)\) is an increasing function.

Indeed, let \(\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n\) (\(n = \mathrm{rgss}(\mathscr{R})\)) be the elements of \(\Delta\). For \(x \in \Gamma_0(R)\), one has a decomposition \[ x = \sum_{i=1}^{n} m_i(x)\alpha_i. \] It suffices to take the lexicographic order relative to the functions \(\sum m_i, m_n, m_{n-1}, \ldots, m_2\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.5.7

The first roots are, in order: \[ \alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n; \] one then has (if these are roots) \(2\alpha_1\), \(\alpha_1 + \alpha_2\), \(\alpha_1 + \alpha_3\), \(\ldots\).
3.6. Weyl chambers

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.6.1

Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb{R}\)-vector space. Let the \(f_i\) be independent linear forms. Put \[ \mathrm{C} = \{x \in V \mid f_i(x) > 0\}. \] Then \(\mathrm{C}\) is a maximal convex subset of \(\mathrm{X} = V - \bigcup_i f_i^{-1}(0)\).
Trivial.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.6.2

A subset \(\mathrm{C}\) of \(V\) which can be described by the procedure of 3.6.1 will be called (here) a chamber of \(V\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.6.3

One says that the hyperplane \(H\) of \(V\) is a wall of \(\mathrm{C}\) if \(H \cap (\overline{\mathrm{C}} - \mathrm{C})\) contains a non-empty open subset of \(H\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.6.4

For a convex subset, the closure can be described without appealing to the topology of \(V\): it is the set of endpoints of all the open segments contained in the given subset.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.6.5

Under the conditions of 3.6.1, one has \[ \overline{\mathrm{C}} = \{x \in V \mid f_i(x) \geqslant 0\}. \] The walls of \(\mathrm{C}\) are the planes \(f_i^{-1}(0)\).

This is clear for the first assertion. The second then follows from the fact that \(\overline{\mathrm{C}} - \mathrm{C} \subset \bigcup_i f_i^{-1}(0)\) and from the fact that the \(f_i^{-1}(0)\) are obviously walls of \(\mathrm{C}\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.6.6

Let \(\mathrm{C}\) be a chamber of \(V\). If \(H_i\), \(i = 1, 2, \ldots n\), are the distinct walls of \(\mathrm{C}\), then for every system of linear forms \(\{u_i\}\) such that \(H_i = u_i^{-1}(0)\), there exist \(\varepsilon_i \in \{-1, +1\}\) such that \(\mathrm{C}\) is defined by \[ \mathrm{C} = \{x \in V \mid \varepsilon_i u_i(x) > 0\}. \] For every wall \(H\) of \(\mathrm{C}\), one has \(H \cap \mathrm{C} = \varnothing\) and \(H \cap \overline{\mathrm{C}} = \overline{\mathrm{C}}_H\), where \(\mathrm{C}_H\) is a chamber in \(H\). The walls of \(\mathrm{C}_{H_i}\) are the \(H_j \cap H_i\), for \(j \ne i\).
This follows trivially from the lemma.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.6.7

The \(\mathrm{C}_{H_i}\) are the faces of \(\mathrm{C}\).
Let now \(\mathscr{R} = (M, M^*, R, R^*)\) be a root datum. One puts \(V^*_{\mathbb{R}} = M^* \otimes \mathbb{R}\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.6.8

For every \(\alpha \in R\), one puts \[ \mathscr{H}_\alpha = \{x \in V^*_{\mathbb{R}} \mid (x, \alpha) = 0\}. \] One writes \(\mathrm{X} = V^*_{\mathbb{R}} - \bigcup_{\alpha \in R} \mathscr{H}_\alpha\). For every \(x \in \mathrm{X}\), one puts \[ R_+(x) = \{\alpha \in R \mid (x, \alpha) > 0\}. \] For every system of positive roots \(R_+\), one writes \[ \mathscr{C}(R_+) = \{x \in V^*_{\mathbb{R}} \mid (x, \alpha) > 0 \quad\text{for all}\quad \alpha \in R_+\}. \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.6.9

(i) For every \(x \in \mathrm{X}\), \(R_+(x)\) is a system of positive roots. For every system of positive roots \(R_+\), \(\mathscr{C}(R_+)\) is a chamber in \(V^*_{\mathbb{R}}\). The \(\mathscr{C}(R_+)\) are the maximal convex subsets of \(\mathrm{X}\).

(ii) Let \(\Delta\) be a system of simple roots. One has \[ \mathscr{C}(\mathscr{P}(\Delta)) = \{x \in V^*_{\mathbb{R}} \mid (x, \alpha) > 0 \quad\text{for all}\quad \alpha \in \Delta\}. \] The walls of \(\mathscr{C}(\mathscr{P}(\Delta))\) are the planes \(\mathscr{H}_\alpha = \alpha^{-1}(0)\), for \(\alpha \in \Delta\); its faces are the \[ \mathrm{C}_\alpha = \{x \in V^*_{\mathbb{R}} \mid (x, \alpha) = 0, \quad (x, \beta) > 0 \quad\text{for}\quad \beta \in \Delta,\ \beta \ne \alpha\}. \]

(iii) One has the equivalence \[ R_+(x) = R_+ \iff x \in \mathscr{C}(R_+). \]

It is clear first of all that \(R_+(x)\) is a system of positive roots. Since \(x \in \mathscr{C}(R_+(x))\), the union of the \(\mathscr{C}(R_+(x))\) is \(\mathrm{X}\). Property (iii) is immediate; it follows that the \(\mathscr{C}(R_+)\) form a partition of \(\mathrm{X}\). The first assertion of (ii) is obvious. It follows at once that \(\mathscr{C}(R_+)\) is a chamber in \(V\), which proves the rest of (ii). It only remains to observe that \[ \bigcup_{\alpha \in R} \alpha^{-1}(0) = \bigcup_{\alpha \in \Delta} \alpha^{-1}(0) \] in order to complete the proof of (i) by 3.6.1.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.6.10

The \(\mathscr{C}(R_+)\) are called the Weyl chambers of the root datum.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.6.11

The maps \(R_+ \mapsto \mathscr{C}(R_+)\) and \(\mathrm{C} \mapsto R_+(x)\) for an arbitrary \(x \in \mathrm{C}\) set up a bijective correspondence between systems of positive roots and Weyl chambers.
This correspondence is invariant under the Weyl group:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.6.12

If \(w \in W(\mathscr{R})\), one has \(\mathscr{C}(w(R_+)) = w(\mathscr{C}(R_+))\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.6.13

The correspondences \(\Delta \leftrightarrow R_+ \leftrightarrow \mathrm{C}\) are isomorphisms of homogeneous spaces under \(W(\mathscr{R})\).
We shall see later that these homogeneous spaces are principal (5.5).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.6.14

If \(\mathrm{C}\) is a Weyl chamber, then so is \(-\mathrm{C}\), called the opposite of \(\mathrm{C}\). There exists therefore a \(w_0 \in W\) (and in fact exactly one, cf. 5.5) such that \(w_0(\mathrm{C}) = -\mathrm{C}\); it is called the symmetry of the root datum relative to the Weyl chamber \(\mathrm{C}\) (or to \(\mathscr{P}(\mathrm{C})\) or to \(\mathscr{S}(\mathscr{P}(\mathrm{C}))\) \(\ldots\)).

pages.title: 4. Reduced root data of semi-simple rank 2

blocks.html: 4. Reduced root data of semi-simple rank 2

Let \(\mathscr{R}\) be a root datum of semi-simple rank 2. Let \(\{\alpha, \beta\}\) be a system of simple roots. Suppose \(\ell(\alpha) \leqslant \ell(\beta)\). By 2.3.1 and 3.2.1 there are then four possibilities:

Type\(\ell(\beta)/\ell(\alpha)\)\(\ell(\beta^*)/\ell(\alpha^*)\)\((\beta^*, \alpha)\)\((\alpha^*, \beta)\)
\(\mathrm{A}_1 + \mathrm{A}_1\)−−\(0\)\(0\)
\(\mathrm{A}_2\)\(1\)\(1\)\(-1\)\(-1\)
\(\mathrm{B}_2\)\(2\)\(1/2\)\(-1\)\(-2\)
\(\mathrm{G}_2\)\(3\)\(1/3\)\(-1\)\(-3\)
It then follows from 3.4.5 that the order of \(s_\alpha s_\beta\) is respectively 2, 3, 4, 6.
Let us study each of these systems separately and give the list of the indivisible roots.
Type \(\mathrm{A}_1 + \mathrm{A}_1\). The indivisible roots are \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), \(-\alpha\), \(-\beta\). The corresponding coroots are \(\alpha^*\), \(\beta^*\), \(-\alpha^*\), \(-\beta^*\).
Type \(\mathrm{A}_2\). The indivisible roots are as follows:

root \(\gamma\)\(\alpha\)\(\beta\)\(\alpha + \beta\)
\(\ell(\gamma)/\ell(\alpha)\)\(1\)\(1\)\(1\)
coroot \(\gamma^*\)\(\alpha^*\)\(\beta^*\)\(\alpha^* + \beta^*\)
\(\ell(\gamma^*)/\ell(\beta^*)\)\(1\)\(1\)\(1\)
The half-sum of the positive indivisible roots is \(\rho = \alpha + \beta\).
Type \(\mathrm{B}_2\). The indivisible roots are the following:

root \(\gamma\)\(\alpha\)\(\beta\)\(\alpha + \beta\)\(2\alpha + \beta\)
\(\ell(\gamma)/\ell(\alpha)\)\(1\)\(2\)\(1\)\(2\)
coroot \(\gamma^*\)\(\alpha^*\)\(\beta^*\)\(2\alpha^* + \beta^*\)\(\alpha^* + \beta^*\)
\(\ell(\gamma^*)/\ell(\beta^*)\)\(2\)\(1\)\(2\)\(1\)
Type \(\mathrm{G}_2\). The indivisible roots are the following:

root \(\gamma\)\(\alpha\)\(\beta\)\(\alpha + \beta\)\(2\alpha + \beta\)\(3\alpha + \beta\)\(3\alpha + 2\beta\)
\(\ell(\gamma)/\ell(\alpha)\)\(1\)\(3\)\(1\)\(1\)\(3\)\(3\)
coroot \(\gamma^*\)\(\alpha^*\)\(\beta^*\)\(\alpha^* + 3\beta^*\)\(2\alpha^* + 3\beta^*\)\(\alpha^* + \beta^*\)\(\alpha^* + 2\beta^*\)
\(\ell(\gamma^*)/\ell(\beta^*)\)\(3\)\(1\)\(3\)\(3\)\(1\)\(1\)
The half-sum of the positive indivisible roots is \(\rho = 5\alpha + 3\beta\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.1

Let \(n\) be the order of \(s_\alpha s_\beta\). Put \(u_0 = 0\) and, for \(p \in \mathbb{Z}_+\), \[ \left\{ \begin{aligned} u_{2p+1} &= u_{2p} + (s_\alpha s_\beta)^p(\alpha)\,; \\ u_{2p+2} &= u_{2p+1} + (s_\alpha s_\beta)^p s_\alpha(\beta). \end{aligned} \right. \] Then:

(i) \(u_{k+2n} = u_k\), \(\qquad k \in \mathbb{Z}_+\)

(ii) \(u_0 = 0\), \(u_1 = \alpha\), \(u_{2n-1} = \beta\), \(u_{2n} = 0\).

(iii) If \(1 < k < 2n - 1\), one has \(u_k = a_k\alpha + b_k\beta\), \(\qquad a_k, b_k \in \mathbb{N}\).

Assertion (i) follows at once from \((s_\alpha s_\beta)^n = 1\) and \(u_{2n} = 0\). Let us prove (ii) and (iii). The computation immediately gives, in the four cases, the following sequences of values:

Type \(\mathrm{A}_1 + \mathrm{A}_1\): \(0, \alpha, \alpha + \beta, \beta, 0\).
Type \(\mathrm{A}_2\): \(0, \alpha, 2\alpha + \beta, 2\alpha + 2\beta, \alpha + 2\beta, \beta, 0\).
Type \(\mathrm{B}_2\): \(0, \alpha, 2\alpha + \beta, 3\alpha + 3\beta, 3\alpha + 4\beta, 2\alpha + 4\beta, \alpha + 3\beta, \beta, 0\).
Type \(\mathrm{G}_2\): \(0, \alpha, 2\alpha + \beta, 4\alpha + 4\beta, 5\alpha + 6\beta, 6\alpha + 9\beta, 6\alpha + 10\beta,\) \(5\alpha + 10\beta, 4\alpha + 9\beta, 2\alpha + 6\beta, \alpha + 4\beta, \beta, 0\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 4.2

(*) Put \(w_{2p} = (s_\beta s_\alpha)^p\), \(w_{2p+1} = s_\alpha(s_\beta s_\alpha)^p\), so that the \(w_i\), \(i = 0, \ldots, 2n - 1\), are the distinct elements of \(W\). Let \(u \in V^*\). One has \[ w_k(u) - u = n_k\alpha^* + m_k\beta^*, \qquad n_k, m_k \in \mathbb{Q}, \] with \(n_k + m_k = -(u, u_k)\).

The proof is by induction on \(k\). If \(k = 0\), the formula is trivially verified. Let us carry out, for example, the passage from \(w_{2p}\) to \(w_{2p+1}\). One has \(w_{2p+1} = s_\alpha w_{2p}\), whence \[ w_{2p+1}(x) - x = s_\alpha w_{2p}(x) - w_{2p}(x) + w_{2p}(x) - x = -(w_{2p}(x), \alpha)\,\alpha^* + n_{2p}\,\alpha^* + m_{2p}\,\beta^*. \] Whence \[ \begin{aligned} n_{2p+1} + m_{2p+1} &= n_{2p} + m_{2p} - ((s_\beta s_\alpha)^p(x), \alpha) \\ &= -(x, u_{2p}) - (x, (s_\alpha s_\beta)^p(\alpha)) = -(x, u_{2p+1}). \end{aligned} \]
(*) The following lemmas 4.2 and 4.4 are used in the proof of 5.1. There are nowadays simpler proofs of 5.1 (see Bourbaki, Groupes et algèbres de Lie, Ch. IV).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.3

If \((u, \alpha) \geqslant 0\), \((u, \beta) \geqslant 0\), and if one puts \[ w(u) - u = a_w r + b_w s, \] one has \(a_w + b_w \geqslant 0\). If moreover \((u, \alpha) > 0\) (resp. \((u, s) > 0\)), then \(a_w + b_w > 0\) for \(w \ne 1\), \(s_\beta\) (resp. \(w \ne 1\), \(s_\alpha\)).
This follows at once from 4.1 and 4.2.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.4

Let \(\mathscr{R}\) be an arbitrary root datum and let \(\Delta\) be a system of simple roots. Let \(\gamma\) be a positive root, and \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) two simple roots. If \[ \mathrm{ord}_\Delta(s_\alpha(\gamma)) < \mathrm{ord}_\Delta(\gamma), \qquad \mathrm{ord}_\Delta(s_\beta(\gamma)) \leqslant \mathrm{ord}_\Delta(\gamma), \] then \(\mathrm{ord}_\Delta(w(\gamma)) \leqslant \mathrm{ord}_\Delta(\gamma)\) for every \(w \in W_{\alpha,\beta}\) (the subgroup of \(W\) generated by \(s_\alpha\) and \(s_\beta\)) and \(\mathrm{ord}_\Delta(w(\gamma)) < \mathrm{ord}_S(\gamma)\) for every \(w \in W_{\alpha\beta}\), \(w \ne 1\), \(w \ne s_\beta\).

Indeed, consider the dual root datum \(\mathscr{R}^*\), then the datum \((M^*, M, R'^*, R')\), where \(R'\) is the set of roots which are rational linear combinations of \(\alpha\) and of \(\beta\). Applying 4.3 to this datum, one finds the announced corollary.

pages.title: 5. The Weyl group: generators and relations

blocks.html: 5. The Weyl group: generators and relations
Let \(\mathscr{R}\) be a root datum. Since the Weyl group is the same for this datum and for the corresponding reduced datum, one may suppose it reduced in order to study the Weyl group.

Let \(\Delta\) be a system of simple roots whose elements will be denoted by \(\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots \alpha_n\), \(n = \mathrm{rgss}(\mathscr{R})\). Let \(n_{ij}\) be the order of the element \(s_{\alpha_i} s_{\alpha_j}\) of \(W\). In particular, one has \(n_{ii} = 1\), and it was seen in 3.4.2 and 3.4.3 that the subgroup \(W_{ij}\) of \(W\) generated by \(s_{\alpha_i}\) and \(s_{\alpha_j}\) was defined by the relations: \[ s^2_{\alpha_i} = s^2_{\alpha_j} = (s_{\alpha_i} s_{\alpha_j})^{n_{ij}} = 1. \]

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.1

The group \(W\) is the group generated by the elements \(s_{\alpha_i}\), \(i = 1, 2, \ldots n\), subject to the relations \((s_{\alpha_i} s_{\alpha_j})^{n_{ij}} = 1\).

We have already seen that the theorem is true when \(n = 2\); we shall make use of this remark in the course of the proof. Let us introduce the group \(\overline{W}\) generated by elements \(T_i\), \(i = 1, 2, \ldots, n\), subject to the relations \((T_i T_j)^{n_{ij}} = 1\). In particular one has \(n_{ii} = 1\), whence \(T^2_i = 1\). Let \(p : \overline{W} \to W\) be the group morphism which sends \(T_i\) to \(s_{\alpha_i}\). It is known that \(p\) is surjective; we are going to show that it is injective.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.2

One can define in a unique manner, for each \(\alpha \in \mathscr{P}(\Delta)\), an element \(T_\alpha \in \overline{W}\) in such a way that the following properties hold:

(i) \(p(T_\alpha) = s_\alpha\),

(ii) \(T_{\alpha_i} = T_i\),

(iii) if \(\beta\) and \(\alpha\) are two positive roots such that \(s_{\alpha_i}(\alpha) = \beta\), then \(T_i T_\alpha T_i = T_\beta\).

Let us first remark that it follows from 1.2.10 and 3.3.6 that (i) is a consequence of (ii) and (iii), and that (ii) and (iii) determine the \(T_\alpha\) completely. We shall carry out the construction by induction on \(\mathrm{ord}_\Delta(\alpha)\). If \(\mathrm{ord}_\Delta(\alpha) = 1\), then \(\alpha \in \Delta\) and one puts \(T_\alpha = T_i\) if \(\alpha = \alpha_i\). Consider the hypothesis:

(H\(_p\)) there exist \(T_\alpha\), for \(\alpha \in \mathscr{P}(\Delta)\), \(\mathrm{ord}_\Delta(\alpha) \leqslant p\), satisfying (ii) and condition (iii) whenever \(\mathrm{ord}_\Delta(\alpha) \leqslant p\), \(\mathrm{ord}_\Delta(\beta) \leqslant p\).

This is satisfied for \(p = 1\): indeed, if \(\alpha\) and \(s_{\alpha_i}(\alpha) = \beta\) are simple, then \(\alpha_i\) and \(\alpha\) are orthogonal, \(\beta = \alpha = \alpha_j\), which gives \[ T_i T_j T_i = T_i, \] by \(n_{ij} = 2\).
Suppose (H\(_{p-1}\)) satisfied.

A) Construction of the \(T_\alpha\) for \(\mathrm{ord}_\Delta(\alpha) \leqslant p\). It clearly suffices to do this for \(\mathrm{ord}_\Delta(\alpha) = p\). There then exists \(\alpha_i \in \Delta\), with \(s_{\alpha_i}(\alpha) \in \mathscr{P}(\Delta)\), \(\mathrm{ord}_\Delta(s_{\alpha_i}(\alpha)) < p\) (3.3.3). One will then put \[ (\star)\qquad T_\alpha = T_i T_{s_{\alpha_i}(\alpha)} T_i. \] Let us verify that \(T_\alpha\) depends only on \(\alpha\). So let \(\alpha_j \in \Delta\) with \(s_{\alpha_j}(\alpha) \in \mathscr{P}(\Delta)\) and \(\mathrm{ord}_\Delta(s_{\alpha_j}(\alpha)) < p\). Let us prove that \[ (\text{+})\qquad T_i T_{s_{\alpha_i}(\alpha)} T_i = T_j T_{s_{\alpha_j}(\alpha)} T_j. \] We distinguish two cases.

(1) Suppose \(\alpha\) is a linear combination of \(\alpha_i\) and of \(\alpha_j\). The same then holds for \(s_{\alpha_i}(\alpha)\) and \(s_{\alpha_j}(\alpha)\), and by (H\(_{p-1}\)), \(T_{s_{\alpha_i}(\alpha)}\) and \(T_{s_{\alpha_j}(\alpha)}\) are written as words in \(T_i\) and \(T_j\). Since the projection of (+) into \(W\) is satisfied, and since the theorem is true for \(n = 2\), so that \(p\) is injective on the subgroup of \(\overline{W}\) generated by \(T_i\) and \(T_j\), (+) is indeed satisfied.

(2) Suppose \(\alpha\) is not a linear combination of \(\alpha_i\) and of \(\alpha_j\). Then if \(w \in W_{\alpha_i\alpha_j}\), the \(w(\alpha)\) will all be positive (cf. 3.4.9). The relation to be verified can also be written \[ (\text{++})\qquad (T_i T_j)^{n_{ij} - 1}\, T_{s_{\alpha_i}(\alpha)}\, (T_j T_i)^{n_{ij} - 1} = T_{s_{\alpha_j}(\alpha)}. \] Now it follows from 4.4 that the \(w(\alpha)\) are all of order \(< p\) for \(w \in W_{\alpha_i\alpha_j}\), \(w \ne 1\). One may therefore apply hypothesis (H\(_{p-1}\)) \(2(n_{ij} - 1)\) times, and we are done.

B) Verification of (H\(_p\)). It only remains to verify the following assertion: if \(\mathrm{ord}_\Delta(\alpha) = p\), \(\mathrm{ord}_\Delta(s_{\alpha_i}(\alpha)) < p\), \(\mathrm{ord}_\Delta(s_{\alpha_j}(\alpha)) = p\), one has \[ (\text{+++})\qquad T_j T_i T_{s_{\alpha_i}(\alpha)} T_i T_j = T_i T_{s_{\alpha_i}(\alpha)} T_i. \] This is done exactly as above.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 5.3

Let \(h \in \overline{W}\). Let us write it \[ h = T_{i_1} \cdots T_{i_p} \cdots T_{i_m} \] in such a way that \(m\) is minimal. Then \[ p(h)(\alpha_m) \in -\mathscr{P}(\Delta). \]

Indeed, since \(h(T_{i_m})(\alpha_m) = s_{\alpha_m}(\alpha_m) = -\alpha_m\), if \(p(h)(\alpha_m)\) were positive, there would exist a \(k\), \(1 \leqslant k \leqslant m - 1\), with \[ u = s_{\alpha_{k+1}} \cdots s_{\alpha_m}(\alpha_m) = -s_{\alpha_{k+1}} \cdots s_{\alpha_{m-1}}(\alpha_m) \in -\mathscr{P}(\Delta), \qquad s_{\alpha_k}(u) \in \mathscr{P}(\Delta). \] But then one necessarily has \(u = -\alpha_k\) (3.3.1), whence \[ s_{\alpha_{k+1}} \ldots s_{\alpha_{m-1}}(\alpha_m) = \alpha_k, \] which entails by (iii) \[ T_k T_{k+1} \cdots T_{m-1} T_m = T_{k+1} \cdots T_{m-1}, \] and contradicts the minimality of \(m\).
Let now \(h \in \overline{W}\) with \(p(h)(\mathscr{P}(\Delta)) \subset \mathscr{P}(\Delta)\). By lemma 5.3, one has \(p(h) = 1\), which proves theorem 5.1 and moreover the

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.4

If \(R_+\) is a system of positive roots and if \(w \in W\) is such that \(w(R_+) = R_+\), then \(w = 1\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.5

The Weyl group operates freely and transitively on the set of systems of positive roots (resp. of systems of simple roots, resp. of Weyl chambers, resp. . . .).

Let us now choose a system of simple roots \(\Delta\). Put \(R^+ = \mathscr{P}(\Delta)\). For every pair of simple roots \((\alpha, \beta) \in \Delta \times \Delta\), let \(R_{\alpha,\beta}\) denote the set of roots which are linear combinations of \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). Write \(R^+_{\alpha,\beta} = R^+ \cap R_{\alpha,\beta}\) and let \(W_{\alpha,\beta}\) be the Weyl group of \(R_{\alpha,\beta}\), that is to say the subgroup of \(W\) generated by \(s_\alpha\) and \(s_\beta\).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.6 (Tits)

Let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be two simple roots and let \(w \in W\) be such that \(w(\alpha) = \beta\). There exists a sequence of simple roots \(\alpha_0, \ldots, \alpha_m\) and a sequence \(w_0, \ldots, w_{m-1}\) of elements of \(W\) satisfying the following conditions:

(i) One has \(\alpha_0 = \alpha\), \(\alpha_m = \beta\).

(ii) One has \(w = w_{m-1} w_{m-2} \cdots w_0\).

(iii) One has \(w_i(\alpha_i) = \alpha_{i+1}\), for \(0 \leqslant i \leqslant m - 1\).

(iv) For every \(i\), \(0 \leqslant i \leqslant m - 1\), such that \(\alpha_i \ne \alpha_{i+1}\), one has \(w_i \in W_{\alpha_i, \alpha_{i+1}}\).

(v) For every \(i\), \(0 \leqslant 1 \leqslant m - 1\), such that \(\alpha_i = \alpha_{i+1}\), there exists a simple root \(\beta_i\) such that \(w_i \in W_{\alpha_i, \beta_i}\).

Put \(M(w) = \mathrm{Card}(P \cap w^{-1}(-P))\). If \(M(w) = 0\), then \(w = 1\) by 5.4 and the theorem is trivial (\(m = 0\), assertions (iii) to (v) being empty). Let us argue by induction on \(M(w)\). If \(M(w) > 0\), there exists \(\beta_0 \in S\) with \(w(\beta_0) \in P\). Put \(\alpha_0 = \alpha\). Consider the set \[ \mathrm{A} = w^{-1}(P) \cap R_{\alpha_0\beta_0}. \] It is a system of positive roots of \(R_{\alpha_0\beta_0}\). There exists therefore \(w_0 \in W_{\alpha_0\beta_0}\) with \[ w_0^{-1}(P_{\alpha_0\beta_0}) = \mathrm{A}. \]

Put \(w' = ww_0^{-1}\). By 3.4.9, one has at once \[ P - P_{\alpha_0\beta_0} = w_0(P - P_{\alpha_0\beta_0}), \] whence \[ (P - P_{\alpha_0\beta_0}) \bigcap w^{-1}(-P) = (P - P_{\alpha_0\beta_0}) \bigcap w'^{-1}(-P). \] On the other hand \[ P_{\alpha_0\beta_0} \cap w'^{-1}(-P) = P_{\alpha_0\beta_0} \cap w_0(-\mathrm{A}) = P_{\alpha_0\beta_0} \cap -P_{\alpha_0\beta_0} = \varnothing, \] whereas \[ \beta_0 \in P_{\alpha_0\beta_0} \cap w^{-1}(-P). \] We have thus proved that \(M(w') < M(w)\). Put \(\alpha_i = w_0(\alpha_0)\); let us show that \(\alpha_1 \in S\), that is to say \(\alpha_0 \in w_0^{-1}(S)\). We know that \(w(\alpha_0) \in S\), hence that \(\alpha_0 \in w^{-1}(S)\), hence also that \(\alpha_0 \in w^{-1}(S) \cap R_{\alpha_0\beta_0}\), hence that \(\alpha_0\) is a simple root of \(\mathrm{A} = w_0^{-1}(P_{\alpha_0\beta_0})\), hence belongs to \(w_0^{-1}(S \cap P_{\alpha_0\beta_0}) \in w_0^{-1}(S)\) (see 3.4.8). We therefore know that \(\alpha_1\) is simple and \(\in R_{\alpha_0\beta_0}\). If \(\alpha_0 \ne \alpha_1\), one thus has \(\beta_0 = \alpha_1\). One has \(\beta = w'(\alpha_1)\), with \(M(w') < M(w)\), and one concludes by induction.
6. Morphisms of root data
6.1. Definition
Let \(\mathscr{R} = (M, M^*, R, R)\) and \(\mathscr{R}' = (M', M'^*, R', R'^*)\) be two root data. Let \(f : M' \to M\) be a linear map and \({}^t f : M^* \to M'^*\) the transposed map.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 6.1.1

One says that \(f\) is a morphism from \(\mathscr{R}'\) to \(\mathscr{R}\), and one writes \(f : \mathscr{R}' \to \mathscr{R}\), if \(f\) induces a bijection of \(R'\) onto \(R\) and \({}^t f\) a bijection of \(R^*\) onto \(R'^*\).
Then \({}^t f\) is a morphism of the dual root data: \[ {}^t f : \mathscr{R}^* \longrightarrow \mathscr{R}'^*. \]

One sees easily that if \(f\) is a morphism from \(\mathscr{R}'\) to \(\mathscr{R}\), and if one writes \(\alpha = f(\alpha')\) for \(\alpha' \in R'\), one has \(\alpha'^* = {}^t f(\alpha^*)\). Indeed, one sees immediately that if \(p\) and \(p'\) denote the maps of 1.2.1 relative to \(\mathscr{R}\) and \(\mathscr{R}'\) respectively, one has \(p' = {}^t f \circ p \circ f\), and the assertion in question follows at once. We leave to the reader the task of proving the statements which follow, and which are almost all trivial.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.1.2

Let \(f : \mathscr{R}' \to \mathscr{R}\) be a morphism of root data. If \(\alpha' \in R'\) and \(\alpha = f(\alpha')\), then \(\alpha'^* = {}^t f(\alpha^*)\). Moreover, \(f\) induces isomorphisms: \[ R' \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} R, \qquad \Gamma_0(R') \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \Gamma_0(R), \qquad \mathscr{V}(R') \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \mathscr{V}(R), \] \({}^t f\) induces isomorphisms: \[ R^* \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} R'^*, \qquad \Gamma_0(R^*) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \Gamma_0(R'^*), \qquad \mathscr{V}(R^*) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \mathscr{V}(R'^*), \] the last being the transpose of the corresponding morphism induced by \(f\). The map \(s_{\alpha'} \mapsto s_{f(\alpha')}\) extends to an isomorphism \(W(\mathscr{R}') \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} W(\mathscr{R})\) compatible with the operations of these two groups on the sets of 1.1.13.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.1.3

The maps \[ \Delta' \mapsto f(\Delta'), \qquad R'_+ \mapsto f(R'_+), \qquad \mathrm{C}' \mapsto ({}^t f \otimes \mathbb{Q})^{-1}(\mathrm{C}') \] define bijective correspondences between systems of simple roots, systems of positive roots and Weyl chambers for \(\mathscr{R}'\) and \(\mathscr{R}\). These correspondences are compatible with the action of the Weyl groups and with the correspondences \[ \mathscr{S}(R_+) \leftrightarrow R_+ \leftrightarrow \mathscr{C}(R_+). \]

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.1.4

Morphisms compose. In order for the morphism \(f : \mathscr{R}' \to \mathscr{R}\) to be an isomorphism, it is necessary and sufficient that \(f : M' \to M\) be bijective.
6.2. Isogenies

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 6.2.1

A morphism \(f : \mathscr{R}' \to \mathscr{R}\) of root data is said to be an isogeny if \(f : M' \to M\) is injective with finite cokernel.
If \(f\) is an isogeny, then \({}^t f\) is an isogeny.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 6.2.2

Let \(f : \mathscr{R}' \to \mathscr{R}\) be an isogeny. We set \(K(f) = \mathrm{Coker}(M' \xrightarrow{\;f\;} M)\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.2.3

There is a natural pairing \[ K(f) \times K({}^t f) \to \mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}, \] which puts these two finite groups in duality.
This is classical.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.2.4

If \(f : \mathscr{R}' \to \mathscr{R}\) is a morphism, then \(\mathrm{rgss}(\mathscr{R}') = \mathrm{rgss}(\mathscr{R})\). If moreover \(f\) is an isogeny, we also have \(\mathrm{rgred}(\mathscr{R}') = \mathrm{rgred}(\mathscr{R})\).
Trivial.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.2.5

Every morphism of semi-simple root data is an isogeny.
This follows at once from the fact that \(f\) must induce an isomorphism of \(V' = \mathscr{V}(R')\) onto \(V = \mathscr{V}(R)\).

If \(\mathscr{R}'\) and \(\mathscr{R}\) are semi-simple, every isogeny \(f : \mathscr{R}' \to \mathscr{R}\) defines a commutative diagram: \[ \xymatrix{ \Gamma_0(R') \ar[r]^-{\sim} \ar@{^{(}->}[d] & \Gamma_0(R) \ar@{^{(}->}[d] \\ M' \ar[r]^-{f} & M. } \] If \(M = \Gamma_0(R)\), then \(f\) is necessarily an isomorphism.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 6.2.6

A root datum is said to be adjoint (resp. simply connected) if \(M = \Gamma_0(R)\), resp. \(M^* = \Gamma_0(R^*)\).

An adjoint or simply connected root datum is therefore semi-simple. \(\mathscr{R}\) is adjoint (resp. s. connected) if and only if \(\mathscr{R}^*\) is s. connected (resp. adjoint). By the preceding result, we have:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.2.7

Let \(\mathscr{R}\) be a semi-simple root datum. The following conditions are equivalent:

(i) \(\mathscr{R}\) is adjoint (resp. simply connected).

(ii) Every isogeny \(\mathscr{R}' \to \mathscr{R}\) (resp. \(\mathscr{R} \to \mathscr{R}'\)) is an isomorphism.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.2.8

Let \(\mathscr{R}\) be an adjoint (resp. simply connected) root datum. Every indivisible root (resp. coroot) is an indivisible element of \(M\) (resp. of \(M^*\)).
Indeed, every indivisible root is part of a basis of \(\Gamma_0(R)\), by 3.3.5.
6.3. Radical and coradical
Let \(\mathscr{R}\) be a root datum. Set \[ \mathrm{N} = \{x \in M \mid (\alpha^*, x) = 0 \quad\text{for all}\ \alpha^* \in R^*\}; \] \[ \mathrm{N}^* = \{M^*/\mathscr{V}(R^*) \cap M^*\}. \]

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.3.1

Consider the canonical morphisms: \[ \mathrm{N} \longrightarrow M, \qquad M^* \longrightarrow \mathrm{N}^*. \] They are transposes of one another and \(\mathrm{N}^*\) is identified with the dual of \(\mathrm{N}\).
This is immediate, taking 1.2.5 into account.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 6.3.2

We call coradical of \(\mathscr{R}\), and denote by \(\mathrm{corad}(\mathscr{R})\), the trivial root datum \[ \mathrm{corad}(\mathscr{R}) = (\mathrm{N}, \mathrm{N}^*, \varnothing, \varnothing). \] If we set \(\mathscr{R}^0 = (M, M^*, \varnothing, \varnothing)\) (this is a trivial root datum), we therefore have a morphism \[ \mathrm{corad}(\mathscr{R}) \longrightarrow \mathscr{R}^0. \]

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 6.3.3

We call radical of \(\mathscr{R}\), and denote by \(\mathrm{rad}(\mathscr{R})\), the trivial root datum: \[ \mathrm{rad}(\mathscr{R}) = \mathrm{corad}(\mathscr{R}^*)^*. \] We therefore have a diagram \[ \xymatrix{ \mathrm{corad}(\mathscr{R}) \ar[rr] \ar[dr] & & \mathrm{rad}(\mathscr{R}) \\ & \mathscr{R}^0 \ar[ur] & } \]
whose transpose is the corresponding diagram for \(\mathscr{R}^*\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.3.4

The canonical morphism \(u : \mathrm{corad}(\mathscr{R}) \to \mathrm{rad}(\mathscr{R})\) is an isogeny.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 6.3.5

We set \(\mathrm{N}(\mathscr{R}) = K(u) = M\big/\big((\mathscr{V}(R) \cap M) + \bigcap_{\alpha \in R} \mathrm{Ker}(\alpha^*)\big)\). We then have a canonical pairing \[ \mathrm{N}(\mathscr{R}) \times \mathrm{N}(\mathscr{R}^*) \longrightarrow \mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}. \]

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.3.6

We have \(\mathrm{rgred}(\mathrm{rad}(\mathscr{R})) = \mathrm{rgred}(\mathrm{corad}(\mathscr{R})) = \mathrm{rgred}(\mathscr{R}) - \mathrm{rgss}(\mathscr{R})\), and the following conditions are equivalent:

(i) \(\mathscr{R}\) is semi-simple,

(ii) \(\mathrm{rad}(\mathscr{R}) = 0\),

(iii) \(\mathrm{corad}(\mathscr{R}) = 0\).
6.4. Products of root data

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 6.4.1

Let \(\mathscr{R} = (M, M^*, R, R^*)\) and \(\mathscr{R}' = (M', M'^*, R', R'^*)\) be two root data. We call the product root datum of \(\mathscr{R}\) and \(\mathscr{R}'\), and denote by \(\mathscr{R}'' = \mathscr{R} \times \mathscr{R}'\), the root datum \((M'', M''^*, R'', R''^*)\) where \(M'' = M \times M'\), \(M''^* = M^* \times M'^*\), \(R'' = R \times 0 \cup 0 \times R'\), \(R''^* = R^* \cup R'^*\) (one regards \(R'' \subset M''\) and \(R''^* \subset M''^*\) in the obvious way, . . .), the map \(\alpha \mapsto \alpha^*\) being the obvious map.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.4.2

Under the preceding conditions we have canonical isomorphisms \[ \Gamma_0(R'') \simeq \Gamma_0(R) \times \Gamma_0(R'), \qquad \mathscr{V}(R'') \simeq \mathscr{V}(R) \times \mathscr{V}(R'), \] \[ W(\mathscr{R}'') \simeq W(\mathscr{R}) \times W(\mathscr{R}'), \] etc..., and relations \[ \mathrm{rgred}(\mathscr{R}'') = \mathrm{rgred}(\mathscr{R}) + \mathrm{rgred}(\mathscr{R}'), \qquad \mathrm{rgss}(\mathscr{R}'') = \mathrm{rgss}(\mathscr{R}) + \mathrm{rgss}(\mathscr{R}'). \] We also have a canonical isomorphism of root data \[ (\mathscr{R} \times \mathscr{R}')^* \simeq \mathscr{R}^* \times \mathscr{R}'^*. \]
The preceding definitions extend at once to a product of several factors. We have at once:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.4.3

Let \(\mathscr{R} = \mathscr{R}_1 \times \mathscr{R}_2 \times \cdots \times \mathscr{R}_n\) be a product of root data. The following conditions are equivalent:

(i) \(\mathscr{R}\) is semi-simple (resp. simply connected, resp. adjoint, resp. reduced).

(ii) Each \(\mathscr{R}_i\) is semi-simple (resp. simply connected, resp. adjoint, resp. reduced).
