Let us consider the following special case: let \(\mathscr{R}_0\) be a trivial root datum and \(\mathscr{R}_1\) a semi-simple root datum. We then have a commutative diagram \[ \xymatrix{ & \mathscr{R}_0 \times \mathscr{R}_1 \ar[dr] & \\ \mathscr{R}_1 \ar[ur] \ar[rr]^-{\mathrm{id}} & & \mathscr{R}_1. } \]

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.4.4

We have canonical isomorphisms \[ \xymatrix{ \mathrm{corad}(\mathscr{R}_0 \times \mathscr{R}_1) \ar[rr]^-{\sim} \ar[dr]_-{\simeq} & & \mathrm{rad}(\mathscr{R}_0 \times \mathscr{R}_1) \\ & \mathscr{R}_0 \ar[ur]_-{\simeq} & } \]
In particular, \(\mathrm{N}(\mathscr{R}_0 \times \mathscr{R}_1) = 0\).
We shall see later that if conversely \(\mathrm{N}(\mathscr{R}) = 0\), then the root datum \(\mathscr{R}\) is the product of a semi-simple datum by a trivial datum.
6.5. Induced and coinduced root data

Let \(\mathscr{R} = (M, M^*, R, R^*)\) be a root datum. Let \(\mathrm{N} \subset M\) be a subgroup containing the roots, i.e., let \[ \Gamma_0(R) \subset \mathrm{N} \subset M. \] The canonical linear map \(i_\mathrm{N} : \mathrm{N} \to M\) gives by transposition a linear map \[ {}^t i_\mathrm{N} : M^* \longrightarrow \mathrm{N}^*. \] Set \(R_\mathrm{N} = R\) and \(R^*_\mathrm{N} = {}^t i_\mathrm{N}(R^*)\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.5.1

\(\mathscr{R}_\mathrm{N} = (\mathrm{N}, \mathrm{N}^*, R_\mathrm{N}, R^*_\mathrm{N})\) is a root datum, and \(i_\mathrm{N}\) a morphism.

Let us first show that \({}^t i_\mathrm{N}\) induces an isomorphism of \(R^*\) onto \(R^*_\mathrm{N}\). If \(\alpha, \beta \in R\) and \({}^t i_\mathrm{N}(\alpha^*) = {}^t i_\mathrm{N}(\beta^*)\), we have \((\alpha^*, x) = (\beta^*, x)\) for all \(x \in \mathrm{N}\), in particular for \(x \in R\), which gives \(\alpha = \beta\) by 1.1.4. The rest follows without difficulty.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 6.5.2

\(\mathscr{R}_\mathrm{N}\) is called the root datum induced by \(\mathscr{R}\) on \(\mathrm{N}\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.5.3

Let \(f : \mathscr{R}' \to \mathscr{R}\) be a morphism. Set \(\mathrm{N} = f(M') \subset M\). Then \(f\) factors uniquely through \(i_\mathrm{N}\).
In particular, the isogenies \(\mathscr{R}' \to \mathscr{R}\), up to isomorphism, correspond bijectively to the subgroups of finite index of \(M/\Gamma_0(R)\), which makes 6.2.7 more precise.

Let now \(\mathrm{N}^*\) be a subgroup of \(M^*\) containing \(R^*\). One defines the datum coinduced by \(\mathscr{R}\) on \(\mathrm{N}^*\) by \[ \mathscr{R}^{\mathrm{N}^*} = (\mathscr{R}^*_{\mathrm{N}^*})^*, \] and one has a canonical morphism: \[ p^{\mathrm{N}^*} : \mathscr{R} \longrightarrow \mathscr{R}^{\mathrm{N}^*}. \]

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.5.4

Let \(f : \mathscr{R}' \longrightarrow \mathscr{R}\) be a morphism. There exist an \(\mathrm{N} \subset M\) and an \(\mathrm{N}'^* \subset M'^*\) such that \(f\) factors as \[ \xymatrix{ \mathscr{R}' \ar[rr]^-{f} \ar[d]_-{p^{\mathrm{N}'}} & & \mathscr{R} \\ \mathscr{R}'^{\mathrm{N}'^*} \ar[rr]^-{f_0}_-{\sim} & & \mathscr{R}_\mathrm{N}, \ar[u]_-{i_\mathrm{N}} } \] where \(f_0\) is an isomorphism.
Indeed, one begins as in 6.5.3. The morphism \(M' \to \mathrm{N}\) obtained is surjective, hence its transpose injective. One takes the image of the latter as \(\mathrm{N}'^*\).

Let us now treat certain special cases. If we take \(\mathrm{N} = \Gamma_0(R)\), we shall write \(\mathscr{R}_\mathrm{N} = \mathrm{ad}(\mathscr{R})\). If we take \(\mathrm{N} = \mathscr{V}(R) \cap M\), we shall write \(\mathscr{R}_\mathrm{N} = \mathrm{ss}(\mathscr{R})\). We therefore have a diagram: \[ \mathrm{ad}(\mathscr{R}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{ss}(\mathscr{R}) \longrightarrow \mathscr{R}. \] By duality, one deduces in the same way a diagram \(\mathscr{R} \to \text{dér}(\mathscr{R}) \to \mathrm{scon}(\mathscr{R})\) where \[ \text{dér}(\mathscr{R}) = \mathrm{ss}(\mathscr{R}^*)^*, \qquad \mathrm{scon}(\mathscr{R}) = \mathrm{ad}(\mathscr{R}^*)^*. \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.5.5

(i) In the diagram \[ \xymatrix{ \mathrm{ad}(\mathscr{R}) \ar[r] & \mathrm{ss}(\mathscr{R}) \ar[rr] \ar[dr] & & \text{dér}(\mathscr{R}) \ar[r] & \mathrm{scon}(\mathscr{R}) \\ & & \mathscr{R} \ar[ur] & & } \] the four data in the first row are semi-simple and the three morphisms are isogenies.

(ii) \(\mathrm{ad}(\mathscr{R})\) is an adjoint datum. \(\mathscr{R}\) is adjoint if and only if \(\mathrm{ad}(\mathscr{R}) \to \mathscr{R}\) is an isomorphism.

(iii) \(\mathrm{scon}(\mathscr{R})\) is a simply connected datum. \(\mathscr{R}\) is simply connected if and only if \(\mathscr{R} \to \mathrm{scon}(\mathscr{R})\) is an isomorphism.

(iv) The following conditions are equivalent:

(a) \(\mathscr{R}\) is semi-simple,

(b) \(\mathrm{ss}(\mathscr{R}) \to \mathscr{R}\) is an isomorphism,

(c) \(\mathscr{R} \to \text{dér}(\mathscr{R})\) is an isomorphism.

Let us pause a moment over the morphism \(\mathrm{ss}(\mathscr{R}) \to \text{dér}(\mathscr{R})\). Referring back to the construction of \(\mathrm{ss}(\mathscr{R})\) and of \(\text{dér}(\mathscr{R})\), it is easy to prove the

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.5.6

Let \(h : \mathrm{ss}(\mathscr{R}) \to \text{dér}(\mathscr{R})\) be the canonical isogeny. We have \(K(h) \simeq \mathrm{N}(\mathscr{R})\).

Let us now consider other special cases of induced data. Set \[ \mathrm{N} = \{x \in M \mid (\alpha^*, x) = 0 \ \text{for}\ \alpha \in R\} \times \Gamma_0(R); \] we know that the sum is direct by 1.2.5. It follows that the root datum \(\mathscr{R}_\mathrm{N}\) is identified with the product \(\mathrm{ad}(\mathscr{R}) \times \mathrm{corad}(\mathscr{R})\).

One may do the same replacing \(\Gamma_0(R)\) by \(\mathscr{V}(R) \cap M\), and then dualise these two constructions. One thus obtains a diagram of root data: \[ \xymatrix@C=0.7em{ \mathrm{ad}(\mathscr{R}) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathrm{ss}(\mathscr{R}) \ar[rr] \ar[d] & & \text{dér}(\mathscr{R}) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathrm{scon}(\mathscr{R}) \ar[d] \\ \mathrm{ad}(\mathscr{R}) \times \mathrm{corad}(\mathscr{R}) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathrm{ss}(\mathscr{R}) \times \mathrm{corad}(\mathscr{R}) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathscr{R} \ar[r] & \text{dér}(\mathscr{R}) \times \mathrm{rad}(\mathscr{R}) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathrm{scon}(\mathscr{R}) \times \mathrm{rad}(\mathscr{R}) \ar[d] \\ \mathrm{ad}(\mathscr{R}) \ar[r] & \mathrm{ss}(\mathscr{R}) \ar[rr] & & \text{dér}(\mathscr{R}) \ar[r] & \mathrm{scon}(\mathscr{R}); } \] which is commutative, as one checks at once. This diagram is self-dual in an obvious sense. The horizontal morphisms are isogenies. The composites of the vertical arrows are the identity.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.5.8

Let \(h_1\) and \(h_2\) be the canonical isogenies: \[ \mathrm{ss}(\mathscr{R}) \times \mathrm{corad}(\mathscr{R}) \xrightarrow{\;h_1\;} \mathscr{R} \xrightarrow{\;h_2\;} \text{dér}(\mathscr{R}) \times \mathrm{rad}(\mathscr{R}). \] We have \(K(h_1) \simeq K(h_2) \simeq \mathrm{N}(\mathscr{R})\).
This is trivial from the definitions.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.5.9

Let \(\mathscr{R}\) be a root datum. The following conditions are equivalent:

(i) \(\mathrm{N}(\mathscr{R}) = 0\), i.e. \(\mathrm{corad}(\mathscr{R}) \to \mathrm{rad}(\mathscr{R})\) is an isomorphism.

(ii) \(h\) is an isomorphism.

(iii) \(h_1\) is an isomorphism.

(iv) \(h_2\) is an isomorphism.

(v) \(\mathscr{R}\) is the product of a semi-simple datum and a trivial datum.
Let us also state a trivial consequence of the preceding remarks:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.5.10

For every root datum \(\mathscr{R}\), there exist isogenies \[ \mathrm{ad}(\mathscr{R}) \times \mathscr{R}_0 \longrightarrow \mathscr{R} \longrightarrow \mathrm{scon}(\mathscr{R}) \times \mathscr{R}_0, \] where \(\mathscr{R}_0\) is "the" trivial root datum of rank \(\mathrm{rgred}(\mathscr{R}) - \mathrm{rgss}(\mathscr{R})\).
Let us finally point out a result which may be useful:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.5.11

Let \(\mathscr{R}\) be a root datum, \(\Delta\) a system of simple roots, \(\Delta'\) a subset of \(\Delta\); consider the root datum (cf. 3.4.7) \[ \mathscr{R}_{\Delta'} = (M, M^*, R_{\Delta'}, R^*_{\Delta'}). \]

(i) If \(\mathscr{R}\) is simply connected, then \(\text{dér}(\mathscr{R}_{\Delta'})\) is simply connected.

(ii) If \(\mathscr{R}\) is adjoint, then \(\mathrm{ss}(\mathscr{R}_{\Delta'})\) is adjoint.

The two assertions are obviously equivalent by duality. The second reduces to checking the formula: \[ M \cap \mathscr{V}(R_{\Delta'}) = \Gamma_0(R_{\Delta'}); \] now, if \(M = \Gamma_0(R)\), both sides are equal to the subgroup of \(M\) generated by \(\Delta'\).
6.6. Weights

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 6.6.1

Let \(\mathscr{R}\) be a root datum. We set \[ \Gamma(\mathscr{R}) = \{x \in V(R) \mid (\alpha^*, x) \in \mathbb{Z} \quad\text{for all}\ \alpha^* \in R^*\}. \] The elements of \(\Gamma(\mathscr{R})\) are called the weights of \(\mathscr{R}\). The weights of \(\mathscr{R}^*\) are called the coweights of \(\mathscr{R}\).
We have \(\Gamma_0(R) \subset \Gamma(\mathscr{R})\) and \(\Gamma(\mathscr{R})\) is stable under \(W(\mathscr{R})\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.6.2

The bilinear map \(V^* \times V \to \mathbb{Q}\) induces a duality \[ \Gamma_0(\mathscr{R}^*) \times \Gamma(\mathscr{R}) \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}. \]
Trivial.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.6.3

Let \(\Delta^* = (\alpha^*_1, \ldots, \alpha^*_n)\) be a system of simple coroots. Let \(p_i\), \(i = 1, 2, \ldots n\), be the elements of \(\mathscr{V}(R)\) defined by \[ (\alpha^*_i, p_j) = \delta_{ij}, \] (whence \(s_{\alpha_i}(p_i) = p_i - \alpha_i\) and \(s_{\alpha_i}(p_j) = p_j\) for \(i \ne j\)) (*). Then \(\Gamma(\mathscr{R})\) is the free abelian group generated by the \(p_i\).
The \(p_i\) are the fundamental weights corresponding to the system of simple coroots \(\Delta^*\).
(*) Warning: if the datum is not reduced, the \(\alpha_i\) do not form a system of simple roots.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.6.4

For every \(\alpha^* \in \Delta^*\), we therefore have \((\alpha^*, \sum_i p_i) = 1\), hence \(\sum_i p_i = \rho_{R_+}\) (cf. 3.5.1), where \(R_+ = \mathscr{P}(\mathrm{ind}(\Delta))\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.6.5

For every \(x \in \mathscr{V}(R)\), we have \(x = \sum_i (\alpha^*_i, x)\,p_i\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.6.6

Note that \(R^* \subset \Gamma_0(R^*)\), \(R \subset \Gamma(\mathscr{R})\), so that \((\Gamma(\mathscr{R}), \Gamma_0(R^*), R, R^*)\) is a root datum. The canonical morphism \(\Gamma_0(R^*) \to M^*\) is the transpose of the morphism \(x \mapsto \sum_i (\alpha^*_i, x)p_i\), which defines a morphism of root data, and we have a commutative diagram: \[ \xymatrix{ & \mathrm{scon}(\mathscr{R}) \ar[d]^-{\wr} \\ \mathscr{R} \ar[ur] \ar[r] & (\Gamma(\mathscr{R}), \Gamma_0(R^*), R, R^*). } \]

We therefore have an explicit description of \(\mathrm{scon}(\mathscr{R})\) in terms of the weights of \(\mathscr{R}\). In the same way, one finds a commutative diagram: \[ \xymatrix{ \mathrm{ad}(\mathscr{R}) \ar[dr] \ar[d]_-{\wr} & \\ (\Gamma_0(R), \Gamma(\mathscr{R}^*), R, R^*) \ar[r] & \mathscr{R}. } \]

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.6.7

In order for \(\mathscr{R}\) to be simply connected, it is necessary and sufficient that \(M = \Gamma(\mathscr{R})\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 6.6.8

We have \(\Gamma(\mathscr{R}) \cap M = \mathscr{V}(R) \cap M\). In order for \(\mathscr{R}\) to be semi-simple, it is therefore necessary and sufficient that \(M \subset \Gamma(\mathscr{R})\).
From the results of 6.5 it also follows that:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.6.9

In order for \(\mathscr{R}\) to be the product of a simply connected datum by a trivial datum, it is necessary and sufficient that \(M \supset \Gamma(\mathscr{R})\).

Let us now consider the canonical isogeny \[ f : \mathrm{ad}(\mathscr{R}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{scon}(\mathscr{R}), \] and set \(\mathrm{Z}(\mathscr{R}) = K(f)\). We have \(\mathrm{Z}(\mathscr{R}) \simeq \mathrm{Z}(\mathrm{scon}\,\mathscr{R}) \simeq \mathrm{Z}(\mathrm{ad}\,\mathscr{R})\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.6.10

We have a canonical isomorphism \(\mathrm{Z}(\mathscr{R}) = \Gamma(\mathscr{R})/\Gamma_0(R)\). More precisely, we have an exact sequence of \(W(\mathscr{R})\)-modules: \[ 0 \longrightarrow \Gamma_0(R) \longrightarrow \Gamma(\mathscr{R}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Z}(\mathscr{R}) \longrightarrow 0. \]

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.6.11

We have a canonical pairing \[ \mathrm{Z}(\mathscr{R}^*) \times \mathrm{Z}(\mathscr{R}) \longrightarrow \mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z} \] which puts these groups in duality.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 6.6.12

We have \(\mathrm{Z}(\mathscr{R} \times \mathscr{R}') \simeq \mathrm{Z}(\mathscr{R}) \times \mathrm{Z}(\mathscr{R}')\). Consider in particular simply connected data \(\mathscr{R}_i\), \(i = 1, 2, \cdots, n\) and a trivial datum \(\mathscr{R}_0\). Set \(\mathscr{R} = \mathscr{R}_0 \times \mathscr{R}_1 \times \cdots \times \mathscr{R}_n\). Let \(\mathscr{R} = (M, M^*, R, R^*)\), \(\mathscr{R}_0 = (M^*_0, M^*_0, \varnothing, \varnothing)\). We have \[ M/\Gamma_0(R) \simeq M_0 \times \mathrm{Z}(\mathscr{R}_1) \times \cdots \times \mathrm{Z}(\mathscr{R}_n). \]
6.7. Automorphisms

An automorphism of \(\mathscr{R}\) is, by 6.1.4, an automorphism of \(M\), say \(u\), such that \(u(R) = R\), \({}^t u(R^*) = R^*\). In particular, every element \(w\) of \(W(\mathscr{R})\) defines an automorphism of \(\mathscr{R}\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.7.1

\(W(\mathscr{R})\) is a normal subgroup of \(\mathrm{Aut}(\mathscr{R})\). More precisely, if \(u \in \mathrm{Aut}(\mathscr{R})\) and \(\alpha \in R\), we have \[ us_\alpha u^{-1} = s_{u(\alpha)}. \]
The proof is the same as that of 1.2.10.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.7.2

Let \(\Delta\) be a system of simple roots. Set \[ \mathrm{E}_\Delta(\mathscr{R}) = \{u \in \mathrm{Aut}(\mathscr{R}) \mid u(\Delta) = \Delta\}. \] Then \(\mathrm{Aut}(\mathscr{R})\) is the semi-direct product of \(W(\mathscr{R})\) by \(\mathrm{E}_\Delta(\mathscr{R})\).

This follows at once from the fact that \(W(\mathscr{R})\) acts simply transitively on the systems of simple roots, and from the fact that if \(\Delta\) is a system of simple roots of \(R\), then \(u(\Delta)\) is a system of simple roots for every automorphism \(u\) of \(\mathscr{R}\).
We shall see later a simpler description of \(\mathrm{E}_\Delta(\mathscr{R})\) in the case of reduced and irreducible root data.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 6.7.3

We denote by \(\mathrm{Aut}^s(\mathscr{R})\) the set of \(u \in \mathrm{Aut}(\mathscr{R})\) such that the following diagram is commutative: \[ \xymatrix{ \mathscr{R} \ar[rr]^-{u} \ar[dr] & & \mathscr{R} \ar[dl] \\ & \mathrm{rad}(\mathscr{R}) & } \]
We write \(\mathrm{E}^s_\Delta(\mathscr{R}) = \mathrm{E}_\Delta(\mathscr{R}) \cap \mathrm{Aut}^s(\mathscr{R})\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 6.7.4

If \(u \in \mathrm{Aut}(\mathscr{R})\), we therefore have \(u \in \mathrm{Aut}^s(\mathscr{R})\) if and only if \((u - \mathrm{id})(M) \subset \mathscr{V}(R)\). In particular \(W(\mathscr{R}) \subset \mathrm{Aut}^s(\mathscr{R})\). It follows at once that:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.7.5

The group \(\mathrm{Aut}^s(\mathscr{R})\) is the semi-direct product of \(W(\mathscr{R})\) by \(\mathrm{E}^s_\Delta(\mathscr{R})\), for every system of simple roots \(\Delta\).

To every automorphism of \(\mathscr{R}\) there is associated by functoriality an automorphism of \(\mathrm{ad}(\mathscr{R})\). We therefore have a canonical morphism \[ \mathrm{Aut}(\mathscr{R}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Aut}(\mathrm{ad}(\mathscr{R})). \]

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.7.6

The morphism \(\mathrm{Aut}^s(\mathscr{R}) \to \mathrm{Aut}(\mathrm{ad}(\mathscr{R}))\) is injective.

Indeed, let \(u\) be an automorphism of \(M\) such that \((u - id)(M) \subset \mathscr{V}(R)\) and such that \({}^t u(\alpha^*) = \alpha^*\) for \(\alpha^* \in R^*\). For every \(x \in M\), we have \[ (\alpha^*, u(x) - x) = ({}^t u(\alpha^*) - \alpha^*, x) = 0, \] hence \(u(x) - x = 0\), by 1.2.5.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.7.7

The group \(\mathrm{Aut}^s(\mathscr{R})\) is finite.

Indeed, it suffices to prove that \(\mathrm{Aut}(\mathscr{R})\) is finite if \(\mathscr{R}\) is adjoint. Since \(M\) is then generated by \(R\), every automorphism of \(\mathscr{R}\) is determined by the permutation of \(R\) which it defines.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 6.7.8

One sees at once that \(\mathrm{Aut}(\mathscr{R})\) (resp. \(\mathrm{E}_\Delta(\mathscr{R})\)) is finite if and only if \(\mathrm{rgred}(\mathscr{R}) - \mathrm{rgss}(\mathscr{R}) \leqslant 1\).
6.8. \(p\)-morphisms of reduced root data
In this no., \(p\) is an integer \(> 0\) fixed once and for all.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 6.8.1

Let \(\mathscr{R} = (M, M^*, R, R^*)\) and \(\mathscr{R}' = (M', M'^*, R', R'^*)\) be two reduced root data. A homomorphism of groups \[ f : M' \longrightarrow M \] is said to be a \(p\)-morphism from \(\mathscr{R}'\) to \(\mathscr{R}\) if the following conditions are satisfied: there exists a bijection \[ u : R \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} R' \] and a map \(q : R \to \{p^n,\ n \in \mathbb{N}\}\) such that:

(i) one has \(f(u(\alpha)) = q(\alpha)\alpha\) for all \(\alpha' \in R'\).

(ii) one has \({}^t f(\alpha^*) = q(\alpha)u(\alpha)^*\) for all \(\alpha \in R\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.8.2

A \(1\)-morphism is nothing other than a morphism.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.8.3

The transpose of a \(p\)-morphism is a \(p\)-morphism.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.8.4

If \(w \in W(\mathscr{R})\), \(\alpha \in R\), one has \(q(w(\alpha)) = q(\alpha)\). The map \(s_\alpha \mapsto s_{u(\alpha)}\) extends to an isomorphism \(\overline{u} : W(\mathscr{R}) \to W(\mathscr{R}')\) such that \[ u(w(\alpha)) = \overline{u}(w)\big(u(\alpha)\big). \]

It suffices to prove that for \(\alpha, \beta \in R\) one has \(u(s_\alpha(\beta)) = s_{u(\alpha)}u(\beta)\) and \(q(s_\alpha(\beta)) = q(\beta)\). Now one has successively: \[ \begin{aligned} f\big(s_{u(\alpha)}u(\beta)\big) &= f(u(\beta)) - (u(\alpha)^*, u(\beta))f(u(\alpha)) \\ &= q(\beta)\beta - q(\beta)q(\alpha)^{-1}(\alpha^*, \beta)q(\alpha)\alpha \\ &= q(\beta)\big(\beta - (\alpha^*, \beta)\alpha\big) = q(\beta)s_\alpha(\beta). \end{aligned} \] If \(\gamma = u^{-1}(s_{u(\alpha)}u(\beta))\), one therefore has \(q(\gamma)\gamma = q(\beta)s_\alpha(\beta)\). The two roots \(\gamma\) and \(s_\alpha(\beta)\) are thus proportional (over \(\mathbb{Q}\)), hence equal or opposite, but \(q(\gamma)\) and \(q(\beta)\) are positive. One therefore has \(q(\gamma) = q(\beta)\) and \(\gamma = s_\alpha(\beta)\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 6.8.5

The \(q(\alpha)\) are called the root exponents of \(f\).

blocks.title: Example
blocks.html:
Example 6.8.6

Let \(\mathscr{R}\) be a reduced root datum and \(q = p^n\). Then \(q : M \to M\) (\(q(x) = qx\)) is a \(p\)-morphism \[ q : \mathscr{R} \longrightarrow \mathscr{R}, \] all of whose root exponents are equal to \(q\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.8.7

With the notation of 6.8.1, \(u\) induces an isomorphism of the set of systems of simple roots (resp. of positive roots) of \(R\) onto the corresponding set for \(R'\).
This follows immediately from 3.1.5 (resp. 3.2.1).
7. Structure
7.1. Decomposition of a root datum

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 7.1.1

Let \(\mathscr{R}\) be a root datum and \(\Delta\) a system of simple roots.

(i) Let \(R'\) and \(R''\) be two closed and symmetric sets of roots forming a partition of \(R\). If one writes \(\Delta' = \Delta \cap R'\), \(\Delta'' = \Delta \cap R''\), then \(R' = R_{\Delta'}\), \(R'' = R_{\Delta''}\), and every root of \(\Delta'\) is orthogonal to every root of \(\Delta''\).

(ii) Let \(\Delta'\) and \(\Delta''\) be two subsets of \(\Delta\) making up a partition of \(\Delta\) and orthogonal. Then \(R' = R_{\Delta'}\) and \(R'' = R_{\Delta''}\) form a partition of \(R\).
Let us first prove (i).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 7.1.2

Under the conditions of (i), if \(\alpha\), \(\beta\) and \(\alpha + \beta\) are roots, all three of them belong to \(R'\) or all three to \(R''\).

Suppose for instance that \(\alpha + \beta \in R'\). Then one cannot have \(\alpha, \beta \in R''\), since \(R''\) is closed; suppose therefore that \(\alpha \in R'\). Then \(-\alpha \in R'\) and \(\beta = (\beta + \alpha) - \alpha \in R'\).

Let us now show that \(R' = R_{\Delta'}\) by induction on the order of a root \(\alpha \in R' \cap \mathscr{P}(\Delta)\). If \(\mathrm{ord}_\Delta(\alpha) = 1\), then \(\alpha \in R' \cap \Delta = \Delta'\). If \(\mathrm{ord}_\Delta(\alpha) > 1\), there exists \(\beta \in \Delta\) with \(\alpha - \beta \in R\). By the lemma, one has \(\beta \in \Delta'\), \(\alpha - \beta \in R'\), hence \(\alpha - \beta \in R_{\Delta'}\) by induction, and finally \(\alpha = (\alpha - \beta) + \beta \in R_{\Delta'}\).

Let us show finally that \(\Delta'\) and \(\Delta''\) are orthogonal. If \(\alpha \in \Delta'\) and \(\beta \in \Delta''\), then \((\beta^*, \alpha) \leqslant 0\). If \((\beta^*, \alpha) \ne 0\), then \(\beta + \alpha\) is a root, contrary to the lemma.

Let us prove (ii). If \(\Delta'\) or \(\Delta''\) is empty, this is immediate. Otherwise, and if \(R_{\Delta'}\) and \(R_{\Delta''}\) do not form a partition of \(R\), there exists a root \(\alpha\) of the form \[ \alpha = \sum m'_i\,\alpha'_i + \sum m''_j\,\alpha''_j, \qquad m'_i \in \mathbb{Z}_+, \quad m''_j \in \mathbb{Z}_+, \] where the \(\alpha'_i\) (resp. \(\alpha''_j\)) denote elements of \(\Delta'\) (resp. \(\Delta''\)). Applying 3.1.2, one deduces from this a relation of the form (after possibly interchanging \(\Delta'\) and \(\Delta''\)): \[ \delta = \gamma + \beta, \quad \gamma \in R_{\Delta'}, \quad \beta \in \Delta'', \quad \delta \in R. \] But since \((\beta^*, \gamma) = 0\), \(\gamma - \beta\) is also a root by 2.2.5, which is impossible.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 7.1.3

Let \(\mathscr{R}\) be a root datum. The following conditions are equivalent:

(i) There is no non-trivial partition of \(R\) into two closed and symmetric subsets.

(ii) For one (resp. every) system of simple roots \(\Delta\) of \(R\), there is no partition of \(\Delta\) into two non-empty orthogonal subsets.

(iii) The natural representation of \(W(\mathscr{R})\) in \(\mathscr{V}(R)\) is irreducible.

(iv) For every pair \((\alpha, \beta)\) of roots, there exists a sequence of roots \(\alpha_0, \alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n\), with \(\alpha = \alpha_0\), \(\alpha_n = \beta\), the roots \(\alpha_i\) and \(\alpha_{i+1}\) (\(i = 0, \ldots, n - 1\)) being non-orthogonal.

One has (i) \(\Leftrightarrow\) (ii) by 7.1.1. One evidently has (iv) \(\Rightarrow\) (ii). Conversely, if (ii) holds for \(\Delta\), condition (iv) holds if \(\alpha, \beta \in \Delta\). Now for every root there exists a simple root not orthogonal to it (3.1.1 for instance). On the other hand (iii) \(\Rightarrow\) (i). Indeed, under the conditions of 7.1.1, \(\mathscr{V}(R')\) is stable under \(W(\mathscr{R})\). It remains to prove (i) \(\Rightarrow\) (iii).

Let then \(H\) be a vector subspace of \(\mathscr{V}(R)\), stable under \(W(\mathscr{R})\). For every \(\alpha \in R\), the equation \(s_\alpha(H) = H\) immediately gives \(\alpha \in H\), or \(\alpha^* \in H^\perp\) (the orthogonal of \(H\) in \(\mathscr{V}(R^*)\) in duality with \(\mathscr{V}(R)\)). If one puts \(R' = \{\alpha \in R \mid \alpha \in H\}\) and \(R'' = \{\alpha \in R \mid \alpha^* \in H^\perp\}\), one has produced a partition of \(R\) into two closed and symmetric subsets.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 7.1.4

A root datum (resp. a root system) satisfying the equivalent conditions of 7.1.3 and of semi-simple rank \(\ne 0\) is said to be irreducible.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 7.1.5

For every root datum \(\mathscr{R}\), there exists a unique partition (up to order) of \(R\) into closed, symmetric and irreducible subsets.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 7.1.6

Every adjoint (resp. simply connected) root datum is a product of irreducible adjoint (resp. simply connected) root data.
It suffices to see this in the adjoint case. The assertion then follows from the fact that under the conditions of 7.1.1, one has \[ \Gamma_0(R) = \Gamma_0(R') \times \Gamma_0(R''). \]

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 7.1.7

For every root datum (resp. and reduced) \(\mathscr{R}\), there exists an isogeny \(\mathscr{R} \to \mathscr{R}'\), where \(\mathscr{R}'\) is a product of a trivial root datum and of irreducible simply connected data (resp. and reduced).
7.2. Properties of irreducible root data

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 7.2.1

Let \(\mathscr{R}\) be an irreducible root datum. For every \(\alpha \in R\), one puts \[ \mathrm{long}(\alpha) = \ell(\alpha)/\ell(\alpha_0); \] where \(\alpha_0 \in R\) is such that \(\ell(\alpha_0)\) is minimal; one says that \(\mathrm{long}(\alpha)\) is the length of \(\alpha\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 7.2.2

Let \(\mathscr{R}\) be an irreducible root datum. The Weyl group operates transitively on the set of roots of the same length.

Indeed, let \(\alpha, \beta \in R\). Since the representation of \(W\) in \(\mathscr{V}(R)\) is irreducible, \(\alpha\) cannot be orthogonal to all the \(w(\beta)\), \(w \in W\). There therefore exists \(w \in W\) with \(w(\beta)\) not orthogonal to \(\alpha\). Now \(\ell(w(\beta)) = \ell(\beta)\) and one concludes by 2.3.2

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 7.2.3

If \(\mathscr{R}\) is irreducible and reduced, then \(\mathrm{long}(R)\) is \(\{1\}\), \(\{1, 2\}\), or \(\{1, 3\}\).

By the remark used above, for all \(\alpha, \beta \in R\), there always exists a \(w \in W\) such that \(w(\beta)\) is not orthogonal to \(\beta\). One therefore has \(\ell(\alpha)/\ell(\beta) = 1, 2, 3, 1/2\) or \(1/3\) (by 2.3.1). One therefore has \(\mathrm{long}(\alpha) = 1, 2\), or \(3\), but if \(\mathrm{long}(\alpha) = 2\), \(\mathrm{long}(\beta) = 3\), then \(\ell(\alpha)/\ell(\beta) = 2/3\), which is impossible.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 7.2.4

Arguing in a similar way, one proves the following result: if \(R\) is irreducible and non-reduced with \(\mathrm{rgss}(\mathscr{R}) > 1\), one has \(\mathrm{long}(R) = \{1, 2, 4\}\). If one puts \(\mathrm{long}^{-1}(i) = R_i\), then \(\mathrm{ind}(R) = R_1 \cup R_2\), \(R_4 = 2R_1\) and two non-proportional roots of \(R_1\) are orthogonal. Conversely, if \(R\) is an irreducible and reduced system such that \(\mathrm{long}(R) = \{1, 2\}\), let us put \(\mathrm{long}^{-1}(i) = R_i\) and suppose that two non-proportional roots of \(R_1\) are orthogonal; then \(R \cup 2R_1\) is irreducible, non-reduced and \(\mathrm{ind}(R \cup 2R_1) = R\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 7.2.5

If \(\mathscr{R}\) is an irreducible root datum, so is \(\mathscr{R}^*\), and \(\mathrm{long}(\alpha)\, \mathrm{long}(\alpha^*) = \mathrm{Cte}\).
This follows immediately from 7.1.3 (iv) and 2.2.6.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 7.2.6

Let \(\mathscr{R}\) be an arbitrary root datum. One calls the length of \(\alpha \in R\), and one denotes by \(\mathrm{long}(\alpha)\), the length of \(\alpha\) in its irreducible component.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 7.2.7

There exists a unique homomorphism of groups \(u : \Gamma_0(R) \to \Gamma_0(R^*)\) such that \(u(\alpha) = \mathrm{long}(\alpha)\alpha^*\) for \(\alpha \in R\).

By 3.5.5, it suffices to check that if \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), \(\alpha + \beta \in R\), one has \[ \mathrm{long}(\alpha)\alpha^* + \mathrm{long}(\beta)\beta^* = \mathrm{long}(\alpha + \beta)(\alpha + \beta). \] But \(\alpha\), \(\beta\) and \(\alpha + \beta\) lie in the same irreducible component of \(R\) by 7.1.2, and one is reduced to 1.2.2.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 7.2.8

For \(\alpha, \beta \in R\), one has \((u(\alpha), \beta) = (u(\beta), \alpha)\). Indeed, this amounts to \[ \mathrm{long}(\alpha)(\alpha^*, \beta) = \mathrm{long}(\beta)(\beta^*, \alpha) \] which is obviously satisfied if \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are orthogonal. If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are not orthogonal, then they lie in the same irreducible component of \(R\), and one is reduced to 1.2.1, formula (9).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 7.2.9

The symmetric bilinear form \((u(x), y)\) is positive non-degenerate on \(\Gamma_0(R)\).

Indeed, let \(R_i\) be the irreducible components of \(R\). One has \[ \Gamma_0(R) = \prod_i \Gamma_0(R_i), \] and the bilinear form \((u(x), y)\) is the product of the forms \[ 2^{-1}\ell(\alpha_i)^{-1}(p(x), y) \] on the \(\Gamma_0(R_i)\), where \(\ell(\alpha_i)\) is the minimum of \(\ell(\alpha)\) for \(\alpha \in R_i\). Now these various symmetric bilinear forms are positive non-degenerate (1.2.6).
7.3. Cartan matrix

Let \(\mathscr{R}\) be a root datum. If \(\Delta\) is a system of simple roots, one calls the Cartan matrix of \(\mathscr{R}\) relative to \(\Delta\) the square matrix over the index set \(\Delta\) defined by \[ a_{\alpha,\beta} = (\alpha^*, \beta); \quad \alpha, \beta \in \Delta. \] Let us first remark that if \(\Delta'\) is another system of simple roots and \(w\) an element of \(W(\mathscr{R})\) such that \(w(\Delta) = \Delta'\), one has \[ (w(\alpha)^*, w(\beta)) = (\alpha^*, \beta), \] so that the Cartan matrix of \(\mathscr{R}\) relative to \(\Delta'\) is obtained from the one relative to \(\Delta\) by the isomorphism \(\Delta \to \Delta'\) on the index set defined by \(w\). It follows that, up to an isomorphism on the index set, the Cartan matrix depends only on \(\mathscr{R}\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 7.3.1

The Cartan matrix has the following properties:

(i) \(a_{\alpha,\alpha} = 2\), \(\qquad a_{\alpha,\beta} \leqslant 0\) for \(\alpha \ne \beta\).

(ii) \(a_{\alpha,\beta} = 0\) implies \(a_{\beta,\alpha} = 0\).

(iii) There exist strictly positive integers \(m_\alpha\) \((= \mathrm{long}(\alpha))\) such that the matrix \[ (m_\alpha\, a_{\alpha,\beta}) \] is symmetric, positive and non-degenerate.

(iv) The diagonal minors of \(a_{\alpha,\beta}\), i.e. the determinants \[ \text{dét}(a_{\alpha,\beta})_{\alpha,\beta \in \Delta'} \quad\text{for}\ \Delta' \subset \Delta, \] are strictly positive.

(v) One has \(s_\alpha(\beta) = \beta - a_{\alpha,\beta}\,\alpha\) and \(s_\alpha(\beta^*) = \beta^* - a_{\beta,\alpha}\,\alpha^*\).

Indeed, (v) is a definition, (i) follows from 3.2.11, (ii) from 2.2.2, (iii) from 7.2.9, and (iv) is deduced immediately from (iii) by the relation \[ \text{dét}(m_\alpha a_{\alpha,\beta})_{\alpha,\beta \in \Delta'} = \Big(\prod_{\alpha \in \Delta'} m_\alpha\Big)\, \text{dét}(a_{\alpha,\beta})_{\alpha,\beta \in \Delta'}. \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 7.3.2

Let \(\mathscr{R}\) and \(\mathscr{R}'\) be two simply connected (resp. adjoint) and reduced root data.

Let \(\Delta\) (resp. \(\Delta'\)) be a system of simple roots of \(\mathscr{R}\) (resp. \(\mathscr{R}'\)), and \(u : \Delta \to \Delta'\) an isomorphism such that, denoting by \((a_{\alpha,\beta})\) and \((a'_{\alpha'\beta'})\) the Cartan matrices of \(\mathscr{R}\) and \(\mathscr{R}'\) relative to \(\Delta\) and \(\Delta'\), one has: \[ a'_{u(\alpha),u(\beta)} = a_{\alpha,\beta}. \] Then there exists a unique isomorphism of \(\mathscr{R}\) onto \(\mathscr{R}'\) inducing \(u\) on \(\Delta\).

It evidently suffices to give the proof in the adjoint case. Then \(M = \Gamma_0(R)\) and \(M' = \Gamma_0(R')\) are the free abelian groups generated by \(\Delta\) and \(\Delta'\). There therefore exists a unique isomorphism of groups from \(M\) onto \(M'\) inducing \(u\) on \(\Delta\). Let us denote it also by \(u\).

Let us show that \(u(R) \subset R'\). Every root \(\alpha\) of \(\mathscr{R}\) is written \(s_{\alpha_1} \cdots s_{\alpha_n}(\alpha_{n+1})\) with \(\alpha_i \in \Delta\). One evidently has \[ u(\alpha) = s_{u(\alpha_1)} \cdots s_{u(\alpha_n)}(u(\alpha_{n+1})), \] in virtue of the hypothesis on \(u\) and of the relations (v) of 7.3.1.

It remains to prove that \({}^t u(R'^*) \subset R^*\), which follows from the fact that the elements of \(M^*\) (resp. \(M'^*\)) are determined by the duality with \(R\) or \(\Delta\) (resp. \(R'\) or \(\Delta'\)), by 1.2.5.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 7.3.3

A reduced simply connected or adjoint root datum is determined up to isomorphism by its Cartan matrix.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 7.3.4

Let \(\mathscr{R}\) be a reduced and simply connected (resp. adjoint) root datum, and \(\Delta\) a system of simple roots. The group \(\mathrm{E}_\Delta(\mathscr{R})\) is identified with the group of automorphisms of the set \(\Delta\) which leave the Cartan matrix invariant.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 7.3.5

The question of the existence of a root datum corresponding to a given Cartan matrix satisfying (i) (ii) and (iv) (for instance) is not easily solved directly, without using the classification.
7.4. Dynkin diagrams

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 7.4.1

By a structure of Dynkin diagram (the word "scheme" has been banished for obvious reasons) on a finite set \(\Delta\), one means the datum of a set of pairs of distinct elements of \(\Delta\), called linked pairs, and of a map from \(\Delta\) to the set \(\{1, 2, 3\}\). The notion of isomorphism of such structures is evident.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 7.4.2

Let \(\mathscr{R}\) be a root datum and \(\Delta\) a system of simple roots. One calls the Dynkin diagram of \(\mathscr{R}\) relative to \(\Delta\) the set \(\Delta\), two simple roots being linked if and only if they are not orthogonal, each root being associated with its length.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 7.4.3

Dynkin diagram and Cartan matrix determine each other bijectively.

Indeed the equivalence \[ \alpha\ \text{and}\ \beta\ \text{are not linked} \iff a_{\alpha,\beta} = 0, \] and the relation \[ \mathrm{long}(\alpha)\, a_{\alpha,\beta} = \mathrm{long}(\beta)\, a_{\beta\alpha}, \] (with \(\inf \mathrm{long}(\alpha) = 1\) in each connected component of the diagram) determine the \(a_{\alpha,\beta}\) in terms of the linkages and the lengths, and conversely (the details of the verification are left to the reader).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 7.4.4

A reduced simply connected or adjoint root datum is determined by its Dynkin diagram.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 7.4.5

Let \(\mathscr{R}\) be a reduced simply connected or adjoint root datum and \(\Delta\) a system of simple roots. The group \(\mathrm{E}_\Delta(\mathscr{R})\) is identified with the group of automorphisms of the Dynkin diagram of \(\mathscr{R}\) relative to \(\Delta\), that is to say with the group of permutations of \(\Delta\) preserving the lengths and the linkages.

7.5. Complements on \(p\)-morphisms

It is clear from the definitions that the bijection \(u : R \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} R'\) associated with a \(p\)-morphism (6.8) makes systems of simple roots, systems of positive roots, irreducible components (etc.) of \(R\) and of \(R'\) correspond to one another. Let us therefore suppose, for simplicity, that \(R\) and \(R'\) are irreducible.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 7.5.1

If \(R\) and \(R'\) are irreducible, then there exists \(k \in \mathbb{Q}\) such that for all \(\alpha \in R\) \[ k\,\mathrm{long}(u(\alpha)) = q(\alpha)^2\,\mathrm{long}(\alpha). \]

Indeed, one has \(\mathrm{long}(\alpha)\,(\alpha^*, \beta) = \mathrm{long}(\beta)\,(\beta^*, \alpha)\) and, likewise, \[ \mathrm{long}(u(\alpha))\,(u(\alpha)^*, u(\beta)) = \mathrm{long}(u(\beta))\,(u(\beta)^*, u(\alpha)). \] One deduces from this at once that for \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) non-orthogonal, one has \[ \frac{q(\alpha)^2\,\mathrm{long}(\alpha)}{\mathrm{long}(u(\alpha))} = \frac{q(\beta)^2\,\mathrm{long}(\beta)}{\mathrm{long}(u(\beta))} \] and one then concludes by 7.1.3 (iv).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 7.5.2

It follows from 7.2.2 and 6.8.4 that \(q(\alpha)\) depends only on \(\mathrm{long}(\alpha)\). One then sees easily that if \(q(\alpha)\) is not constant, then \(q(\alpha)\,\mathrm{long}(\alpha)\) is constant, which shows that then \(p = 2\) or \(3\). A glance at the diagrams of the preceding no. shows that there are four possible cases (one designates by the same letter a Dynkin diagram and the corresponding reduced simply connected root datum): \[ \begin{aligned} p = 2, &\qquad \mathrm{B}_n \xrightarrow{\;f_1\;} \mathrm{C}_n, \qquad \mathrm{C}_n \xrightarrow{\;f_2\;} \mathrm{B}_n \qquad (\text{with}\ \mathrm{C}_2 = \mathrm{B}_2). \\ p = 2, &\qquad \mathrm{F}_4 \xrightarrow{\;g\;} \mathrm{F}_4. \\ p = 3, &\qquad \mathrm{G}_2 \xrightarrow{\;h\;} \mathrm{G}_2. \end{aligned} \] The reader will notice that \(f_1 \circ f_2\), \(f_2 \circ f_1\), \(g \circ g\) and \(h \circ h\) are \(p\)-morphisms of the form described in 6.8.6.

One sees at once from the preceding description that if \(\mathscr{R}\) and \(\mathscr{R}'\) are two reduced root data of semi-simple rank \(\leqslant 2\) and if one has a \(p\)-morphism from \(\mathscr{R}'\) to \(\mathscr{R}\), then \(\mathscr{R}\) and \(\mathscr{R}'\) are of the same type.
